articles.title: ABP completes storage facility at the port of King’s Lynn
articles.summary: Associated British Ports has completed a GBP 7 million investment in a new build-to-suit storage and processing facility at the Port of King’s Lynn for speciality chemical and food ingredients business Azelis. It is ABP’s largest investment at the port to date and supports the growth of its relationship with Azelis,...
articles.body: Associated British Ports has completed a GBP 7 million investment in a new build-to-suit storage and processing facility at the Port of King’s Lynn for speciality chemical and food ingredients business Azelis. It is ABP’s largest investment at the port to date and supports the growth of its relationship with Azelis, which already operates from Teignmouth and Garston. The facility stands at the junction of Edward Benefer Way and Estuary Road and comprises about 4,600 square metres of storage for loose salt and bagged products, plus roughly 5,000 square metres of heavy-duty concrete yard. Azelis operates it under a lease with ABP and has installed a robotic plant on site, bringing storage, processing and distribution together at the port for more efficient cargo handling and supply chain operations. The site was previously redundant, and its reuse shows ABP’s build-to-suit approach of combining development expertise, available port land and operational infrastructure to deliver purpose-built facilities around customers’ requirements. Britcon built the facility, which includes LED lighting, about 3,000 tonnes of recycled aggregate and a sustainable surface-water drainage system. It is also the first bulk storage warehouse in East Anglia delivered through ABP’s industrial frameworks contract. King’s Lynn specialises in agribulks, forest products and construction materials and forms part of ABP’s East Anglian ports with Ipswich and Lowestoft, which together with their customers contribute GBP 360 million a year to the UK and support 5,300 jobs. James Wild, MP for North West Norfolk, called the investment a strong vote of confidence in the local economy and welcomed the return of an underused part of the port to productive use. Paul Ager, Divisional Port Manager at ABP, described it as a major milestone that supports customers’ long-term growth and King’s Lynn’s role in regional supply chains. Kevin Fosbury, Property Asset Manager, and Matt Young, Lead Property Development Manager, both highlighted the collaboration between ABP’s teams in delivering a bespoke facility, with Young noting that ABP is increasingly looking to replicate the model across its estate.

articles.body: Coast Guard Awards Contracts for Coast Guard Academy Construction, Renovation Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 © Wangkun Jia - stock.adobe.com The U.S. Coast Guard awarded a $155 million contract to The Whiting-Turner Contracting Co., of Greenbelt, Maryland, to construct a new Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics facility at the U.S. Coast Guard Academy. The contract, awarded Nov. 16, is one month ahead of schedule and supports the Coast Guard’s ongoing effort to modernize Academy facilities and prepare future officers for service in a technologically advanced maritime environment. The approximately 120,000 square-foot facility, commonly known as STEM West, will include laboratories, classrooms and design spaces supporting the Academy’s engineering curriculum. It will serve as the future home of the Coast Guard’s chemistry; naval architecture and marine engineering; and civil and environmental engineering programs. The accelerated design-build-to-budget contract will incorporate stakeholder input as the final design is completed. Construction is expected to conclude in spring 2030. The STEM West award also marks a Coast Guard-wide milestone. The service has now obligated $20 billion of the nearly $25 billion in funding provided through the Working Families Tax Cuts Act. Separately, the Coast Guard awarded a $29.3 million contract Sept. 29 to Healtheon Inc., of New Orleans, to repair, renovate and reconfigure Waesche Hall. Funded through the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, the project is expected to be completed in May 2029. The Waesche Hall project will modernize approximately 40,000 square feet of the building’s 60,000-square-foot footprint. Planned work includes repairs to bathrooms, faculty offices, classrooms, high-density bookshelves and Admissions Department spaces. The project also includes reconfiguring the first-floor museum exhibit area to accommodate a projection screen and temporary foldable assembly seating. On the second floor, the renovation will add three classrooms, library space, offices and academic department spaces. The improvements will enhance areas used by cadets for collaboration and study, including dedicated space for teaching and learning. The projects are part of a broader Academy modernization effort that includes construction of a new aquatics center and parking garage, as well as improvements to cadet living conditions in Chase Hall. In August, the Coast Guard awarded a $51 million contract to renovate Chase Hall Annex A. Founded in 1876, the U.S. Coast Guard Academy is one of five federal service academies. Each year, approximately 200 graduates are commissioned as Coast Guard officers and begin serving in America’s multi-mission maritime military force.

articles.title: Clean tankers freight slumps as Persian Gulf transits slow amid attacks
articles.summary: Medium Range, or MR, tanker freight across Asia-Pacific slumped Nov. 18, falling w125 on a benchmark route from the Middle East due to slower oil flows through the risky waters of the Strait of Hormuz, market participants said. “Cargo flows are limited; there are hardly any refined products coming out from the...
articles.body: Clean tankers freight slumps as Persian Gulf transits slow amid attacks in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 Medium Range, or MR, tanker freight across Asia-Pacific slumped Nov. 18, falling w125 on a benchmark route from the Middle East due to slower oil flows through the risky waters of the Strait of Hormuz, market participants said. “Cargo flows are limited; there are hardly any refined products coming out from the Persian Gulf. Several tankers are looking for employment and ready to snap up cargoes at lower rates,” said a senior executive with a clean oil tanker owner whose ships load cargoes that transit through the Strait of Hormuz via ship-to-ship, STS transfers in Duqm, Sohar and Fujairah. The Torm Stellar was placed on subjects at w500 by Vitol for Nov. 25 diesel loading on the benchmark Duqm-East Africa route, several brokers said. It was followed by taking another MR, the Weco Amalie, at w475 for loading next week on the Sikka-East Africa route, they said. This is w125 lower than the previous fixture on a similar route, according to S&P Global Platts’ heard and fixtures data. The downside is expected to continue in the near term due to geopolitical concerns and a buildup of tankers, brokers said. Only a small number of companies permit their tankers and crew to transit through the dreaded Strait of Hormuz, while the rest either seek employment in other regions or wait for tankers inside the Strait to bring out cargoes for STS transfers in Oman and West Coast India, according to executives of shipping enterprises and tanker brokerages. Demand for such STS transfers has declined considerably in the last two weeks, said two tanker brokers in the UAE, citing the looming threat of attacks during transit in the Persian Gulf. Three commercial ships were attacked in the Persian Gulf and waters off Oman in the last two days, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations. Tankers have to wait for an opportune moment to exit the Persian Gulf, and due to increased attacks, transits are slowing, said a chartering executive in Singapore. Daily transits through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to only 14 ships on Nov. 9, down from 32 ships at the end of October, according to data from S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab). According to shipping brokers, an average of fewer than half a dozen refined-products tankers manage to come through the Strait on any given day. Weakness in long-range, or LR, tankers is also dragging down overall freight, market participants said. According to Platts data, the benchmark Persian Gulf-North Asia LR1 freight rate has not been assessed higher day-over-day for almost a month now. The weakness is having a cascading effect in other regions as well, market participants added. There has been a slump in loadings in North Asia as refined products shipped from China have turned out to be lower than anticipated, they said. Even though China announced an additional round of export quotas of about 5.65 million mt late last month, actual shipments have not been commensurate with the executive fiat, they said. The situation can change if utilization of such export quotas revives for loadings next month, as companies need to cover their high crude costs by recording more sales before quarterly and annual accounts close, said a chartering executive in Tokyo. The Oriental Sunstone was placed on subjects at $975,000 by Idemitsu for end-November loading on the South Korea-Japan route, several brokers said. This is the first time since end-August that a deal has been done below the key psychological mark of $1 million on this route, Platts data showed. The route has not been assessed higher day over day since Nov. 4, the same data showed. Due to lower MR freight rates, some charterers are considering the option of downsizing their LR cargoes or splitting them into smaller parcels, said brokers directly involved in such deals. Brokers cited the example of Sitme’s 60,000 mt jet fuel cargo, which is likely to be split and loaded on MRs on the STS Sohar-UKC route. Source: Platts 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Ship Recycling Markets Looking Stronger
articles.summary: The ship recycling markets have regained momentum over the past week. In its latest weekly report, Best Oasis (www.best-oasis.com), a leading cash buyer of ships said that “the Indian ship recycling market has started to regain momentum following the five-day Diwali holiday break, with market activity gradually...
articles.body: Ship Recycling Markets Looking Stronger in Hellenic Shipping News 19/11/2026 T he ship recycling markets have regained momentum over the past week. In its latest weekly report, Best Oasis ( www.best-oasis.com ), a leading cash buyer of ships said that “the Indian ship recycling market has started to regain momentum following the five-day Diwali holiday break, with market activity gradually picking up.Local steel demand is expected to improve as markets return to normal operations, supporting renewed buying interest among recyclers. Buying indications are expected to strengthen further in the coming week as demand improves and market activity gathers pace. Overall, market sentiment remains positive, with expectations of firmer prices and improved buying activity in the near term. The Bangladeshi ship recycling market continues to attract strong buying interest, with recyclers remaining keen to acquire suitable tonnage. However, local market conditions have softened over the past few days, putting some downward pressure on price indications. Despite the recent softening, buyers remain keen to secure suitable recycling candidates, with buying interest continuing at competitive levels. Overall, market sentiment remains cautiously positive, supported by sustained buying interest despite the recent weakness in local market conditions”. Best Oasis added that “the Pakistani ship recycling market remains largely unchanged this week, with limited movement in local market conditions and demand. Although buyers remain present, the availability of suitable recycling tonnage continues to be limited. Several recyclers who were previously keen to acquire vessels have now adopted a wait-and-see approach, anticipating a correction in vessel prices before re-entering the market. Overall, market sentiment remains subdued, with buying activity expected to remain selective until more competitively priced tonnage becomes available. Finally, the Turkish ship recycling market remains stable but subdued, with limited vessel availability and cautious purchasing activity. Recyclers continue to face pressure from weak domestic steel demand, elevated financing costs and ongoing currency depreciation. Buying prices remain relatively uncompetitive compared with India, Bangladesh and Pakistan, limiting Türkiye’s ability to attract conventional recycling tonnage. Nevertheless, Türkiye retains a competitive position in recycling EU-linked vessels, supported by its proximity to Europe and established environmental compliance standards. Overall, market sentiment remains cautious, with recyclers adopting a wait-and-see approach as they await an improvement in domestic steel demand. Buying activity is expected to remain limited in the near term”, the report concluded. In a separate note this week, shipbroker Intermodal commented that “last week, recycling markets held back with India remaining firm and Bangladesh showing the strongest appetite for conventional tonnage across the Subcontinent. Against this backdrop, Best Oasis became the second cash buyer, after GMS, to obtain OFAC approval for negotiating transactions involving sanctioned tonnage. Alang’s sentiment continues to be positive. Local steel prices edged slightly over the week amid a sluggish market. However, as activity is slowly recovering after the holiday slowdown, buyers’ appetite is expected to firm. Local currency rate weakened against the USD, due to increased trade deficit driven by festive demand for gold. Few candidates were circulated to the market, among them a mining vessel. Interest in conventional units shows no sign of fading, although breakers are taking a careful line on commitments, as there is uncertainty over the finalization of the EU approval list. Source: Intermodal shipbroker Chattogram’s sentiment was selective, but positive, with continuous appetite on tonnage acquisitions. Local steel prices declined with mills cautiously considering further purchases, as expectations grow that public infrastructure projects will continue. Local currency rate strenghtened against the USD, as Bangladesh Bank sold 200m of its USD reserves to support Taka. Few dry candidates were circulated to the market, with conventional vessels keeping interest strong. Gadani remained static, with market participants being cautious about an expected correction. Overall local market conditions are subdued with local steel market remaining slow. Local currency firmed slightly against the USD. Dry tonnage has been circulated to the market, but breakers seem unwilling for further purchases. Aliaga retains the selective approach over subdued market conditions. The explosion at Habas iron and steel plant created further concerns on steel supply, increasing HRC and Hollow product prices. Weak steel demand, high financing costs and currency depreciation still weigh on sentiment, while the national central bank revised forecasts for 2026 inflation to 29.50%”, the shipbroker concluded. articles.title: Shipping industry urges governments to agree on global GHG regulations to provide regulatory certainty and incentivize maritime decarbonization
articles.summary: In advance of the UN International Maritime Organization (IMO) Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85), which meets in London from 30 November to 4 December 2026, this statement is made jointly by BIMCO, CLIA, IBIA, ICS, INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO, IPTA and WSC representing the global commercial...
articles.body: Shipping industry urges governments to agree on global GHG regulations to provide regulatory certainty and incentivize maritime decarbonization in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 19/11/2026 I n advance of the UN International Maritime Organization (IMO) Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85), which meets in London from 30 November to 4 December 2026, this statement is made jointly by BIMCO, CLIA, IBIA, ICS, INTERCARGO, INTERFERRY, INTERTANKO, IPTA and WSC representing the global commercial shipping fleet. The global shipping industry welcomes continuing efforts by all IMO Member States to agree on a global framework of practical, effective and fit for purpose regulations to help decarbonize international shipping and, whilst further improving energy efficiency, continue striving towards the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy goal of net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by or close to 2050. The industry recognizes that all proposals put forward by governments, and the elements these contain, remain under consideration, but emphasizes the importance of an achievable, enforceable, and stable regulatory framework which reflects cost and availability and provides clear incentives for the development and deployment of commercially viable alternative fuels. The regulatory framework must also meaningfully support a safe energy transition through solutions which are data-driven and fuel and technology neutral. Shipping is a global industry requiring global rules applied equally to all ships, regardless of flag, ownership, trade or business model. A coordinated global approach at IMO must lead to the avoidance of regulatory fragmentation or regional or national measures which result in duplication of compliance requirements for ships or multiple charges for the same GHG emissions. During the transition to lower-GHG fuels, only global regulation can ensure a level playing field. The GHG reduction regulations to be adopted by IMO Member States must reward verifiable emission reductions and incentivize, financially and/or technically, further investments that advance maritime decarbonization. In addition, the regulations should also provide optional/flexible compliance mechanisms so that shipping companies, large and small, can manage the transition, recognizing the current unavailability of commercially viable zero/near-zero GHG fuels and technologies (ZNZs) for the majority of the existing fleet. The shipping industry has invested billions of dollars in new ships capable of using alternative low GHG fuels, innovative technologies, and fuel-flexible solutions. The regulatory framework must support credible transition pathways for existing ships and technologies. Continued industry investment and effective implementation will depend on global regulatory certainty and the reliable production and cost-competitiveness of alternative fuels at scale. Shipowners and other maritime stakeholders, including marine fuel producers, charterers, ports and financiers, all need investment certainty to support the maritime energy transition. An effective global regulatory framework agreed at the IMO is essential to provide clear predictable production pathways for further emissions reductions. To drive decarbonization across the shipping industry, support fleet renewal and financing decisions and maintain a global level playing field, the framework must be pragmatic, fit for purpose and underpinned by clear and enforceable obligations. This framework needs to be agreed as soon as practicable by the industry’s global regulator, the IMO. Achieving an agreement at IMO will require constructive engagement by all Member States, on all sides of the debate, with the full range of alternative proposals on the table, to identify areas of convergence and to draw on their most effective elements, so as to develop a global solution that takes into account strategic ambition as well as market and technological readiness. The shipping industry remains committed to working constructively with all IMO Member States to finalize a meaningful and effective global regulatory framework supported by the development of foundational technical guidance, including on fuel certification and GHG lifecycle assessment. Advancing practical, enforceable and globally consistent solutions is required to ensure that this hard-to-abate sector is able to decarbonize as soon as possible through a safe and sustainable transition. Source: International Chamber of Shipping Tops 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.summary: “In October 2026, Guinea became the world’s third-largest iron ore exporter, with exports surpassing 5m tonnes for the first time and accounting for 3% of global iron ore volumes. The country has gradually ramped up shipments following the start of mining operations at Simandou in December 2025. More than 22m tonnes...
articles.body: Guinea climbs to third-largest iron ore exporter as shipments surpass 5m tonnes in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 19/11/2026 “I n October 2026, Guinea became the world’s third-largest iron ore exporter, with exports surpassing 5m tonnes for the first time and accounting for 3% of global iron ore volumes. The country has gradually ramped up shipments following the start of mining operations at Simandou in December 2025. More than 22m tonnes have been shipped so far in 2026, already surpassing initial industry projections of around 20m tonnes for the full year,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO. The Simandou mining project is in southeastern Guinea and contains one of the world’s largest deposits of high-grade iron ore. Once fully ramped up, the project is expected to have an annual capacity of around 120m tonnes, equivalent to an average of 10m tonnes per month. With exports surpassing 5m tonnes in October, Guinea has already reached around half of Simandou’s planned monthly capacity. Full capacity is projected to be reached towards the end of the decade, although the exact timescale remains uncertain. “Guinean iron ore exports are particularly beneficial for ship demand, as they typically travel 88% longer distances than the average iron ore shipment. Consequently, the exports accounted for 6% of global iron ore tonne-mile demand in October. Overall, the increase in Guinean shipments contributed to a 2% y/y increase in global iron ore tonne miles between January and October, despite stagnant cargo volumes,” says Gouveia. Guinean iron ore has headed almost exclusively to China, the world’s largest iron ore importer. China relies on a combination of high-grade imported iron ore and domestic supplies, which are often of a lower grade, to supply its steel industry. So far this year, China’s steel production has fallen 3% y/y due to weaker demand, while iron ore shipments to the country have risen 1% y/y. Growing supply from major exporters, including Guinea, has weighed on iron ore prices, making imported ore increasingly competitive with domestic Chinese mining. At the same time, lower prices have intensified competition among exporters, prompting some smaller Brazilian miners to reduce output amid weaker prices and high freight costs. “Simandou could have a significant impact on capesize ship demand, even if its exports partly displace existing iron ore trade. Global iron ore tonne-mile demand could rise 13% compared with 2025 if Guinean exports reach 120m tonnes while other exporters maintain their volumes. Even if every additional Guinean tonne replaces an existing shipment, the longer sailing distances could still increase tonne-mile demand by around 6%,” says Gouveia. articles.title: Iran’s Hormuz blacklist reshapes flows, but exports hold
articles.summary: Iran has designated more than half the tankers involved in Gulf shuttle operations, but so far the restrictions have not reduced the volume of oil moving through the shuttle relay. Instead, Vortexa data indicates that operators are adapting how cargoes move, with some designated vessels relying on an additional...
articles.body: Iran’s Hormuz blacklist reshapes flows, but exports hold in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 Iran has designated more than half the tankers involved in Gulf shuttle operations, but so far the restrictions have not reduced the volume of oil moving through the shuttle relay. Instead, Vortexa data indicates that operators are adapting how cargoes move, with some designated vessels relying on an additional ship-to-ship (STS) transfer to get oil to its final destination. Key takeaways • More than half the shuttle fleet has been designated. Of the 231 tankers involved in Gulf shuttle operations since March (excluding Iran), 130 appear on the 2 November PGSA Non-Compliance List. These vessels have accounted for approximately three-quarters of shuttle runs. • Iran has targeted the busiest ships. 89% of tankers with seven or more shuttle runs are on the list, against 26% of those that made a single run. • Designated vessels continue to load in the Gulf. Cargoes carried by the 33 shuttle tankers listed by 14 September averaged 2.1mbd between 15 September and 25 October, up from 1.5mbd in June–July. That 42% rise was in line with tankers not yet listed. • Hormuz transits have slowed relative to the wider fleet. Designated tankers’ weekly transits were flat or down after listing, while transits by all oil tankers rose about 30% over the same before-and-after weeks. • Second STS transfers are becoming more common. On tankers listed by 14 September, about one in five relayed barrels went through a second STS transfer after listing in the Gulf of Oman, up from one in six before. On tankers not yet listed, the rate fell to one in ten. • Gulf shuttle volumes continue to grow. Oil movements through the relay increased from 5.7mbd in August to 8.5mbd in October (excluding Iran), suggesting that operators have so far been able to adapt to the restrictions. Iran’s designations now cover the majority of shuttle activity Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) expanded its Non-Compliance List on 2 November, adding 114 vessels and bringing the published total to 240. Of the 231 tankers Vortexa has identified as participating in Gulf shuttle operations since March, 130 were included in that version of the list, representing 56% of the fleet. These vessels account for a disproportionate share of shuttle activity, having performed approximately three-quarters of all runs between Gulf loading terminals and STS locations east of Hormuz. The designated shuttle fleet is dominated by large crude carriers, including 86 VLCCs, alongside Suezmaxes, Aframaxes and product tankers. Iran has targeted the busiest ships, not one exporter What sets the designated tankers apart is how active they have been in the relay, not where they load. Only 26% of tankers that made a single shuttle run since March are on the list, against 86% of those with four to six runs and 89% of those with seven or more. Listed tankers averaged 4.2 runs each, against 1.7 for those left off. The scale of these designations raises an important question for the market: are restrictions actually reducing Gulf oil exports, or are they changing how cargoes move? Designated tankers continue to load Gulf crude Despite the restrictions, Vortexa data shows that designated tankers have continued to load significant volumes of oil from Gulf terminals. The 33 shuttle tankers designated by 14 September loaded an average of 2.1mbd between 15 September and 25 October, up from approximately 1.5mbd in June–July. This increase was broadly consistent with the 36% growth recorded among a comparison group of 20 shuttle tankers that were not designated until 2 November. In other words, the earlier-designated vessels have not experienced an evident decline in loading activity relative to their peers. However, the picture is different when looking at Strait of Hormuz transit activity. For shuttle tankers designated between 24 August and 2 September, weekly transits averaged 10.3 after listing, compared with 10.8 beforehand. Over the same period, transits across the wider oil-tanker fleet increased by 32%. The divergence was more pronounced among vessels designated between 14 September and October. Their weekly transits declined by 28%, from 21.7 to 15.6, while the wider fleet recorded a 31% increase. Shuttle runs to STS locations east of Hormuz also declined for both groups, by 22% and 29%, respectively. This suggests that designated tankers are making fewer voyages through Hormuz relative to overall market activity, even as they continue to load Gulf crude. The distinction matters. The data points to changes in vessel deployment and cargo movements, rather than a straightforward reduction in exports. However, the observed divergence does not by itself establish that PGSA designations caused the slowdown. Additional STS transfers are emerging in cargo movements One of the more notable developments is the increasing use of additional STS transfers involving designated vessels. For shuttle tankers designated by 14 September, Vortexa estimates that the share of relayed barrels involving a second STS transfer increased from 17% in June–July to 21% between 15 September and 25 October. While additional STS transfers became more common among designated tankers, the opposite trend was observed among vessels that had not yet been designated. For these vessels, the estimated share of cargo requiring a second STS transfer declined from 23% in June–July to 10% between mid-September and late October. For example, Vortexa tracked a designated VLCC that loaded crude at a Gulf terminal in early September before transferring its cargo to a non-designated tanker off Fujairah. Rather than transporting the oil directly to its final destination, the receiving tanker subsequently split the cargo between two additional vessels, which delivered the oil to China and Singapore. This illustrates how operators can introduce an additional step into the cargo movement, allowing designated shuttle tankers to continue loading and transferring Gulf crude while relying on other vessels for onward transportation. Vortexa data also indicates that the use of such intermediate vessels is becoming more common. One non-designated tanker, which had not handled cargoes from the early-designated fleet during June–July, was involved in the onward movement of portions of 10 cargoes between mid-September and late October. What does this mean for Gulf oil exports? The data so far suggests that Iran’s restrictions are having a greater impact on how oil moves than on how much oil moves. Designated tankers continue to load Gulf crude, and overall shuttle volumes have increased even as the number of vessels on the PGSA list has expanded. At the same time, lower relative transit activity among designated vessels and the increasing use of additional STS transfers point to adjustments within the physical supply chain. The next test will be whether these arrangements remain sustainable as the latest designations begin to affect cargo movements. Three developments will be particularly important to monitor: • The impact of the 2 November designations. The addition of 73 shuttle tankers more than doubled the designated shuttle fleet. Their subsequent movements will help establish whether the use of additional transfers becomes more widespread. • The emergence of new intermediate vessels. Greater reliance on a smaller pool of non-designated tankers could increase vessel requirements and introduce new operational bottlenecks. • Changes in direct deliveries and shuttle utilization. A sustained shift towards direct voyages, or longer turnaround times for shuttle vessels, could change the capacity and structure of the Gulf relay system. For now, the expansion of the PGSA blacklist has not translated into a corresponding reduction in Gulf shuttle volumes. Instead, Vortexa data suggests that the market is absorbing the restrictions through changes in vessel deployment and cargo transfer patterns. The question is how much additional complexity the relay can absorb before it begins to affect the volume or speed of Gulf oil exports. Source: Vortexa 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Instead, Vortexa data indicates that operators are adapting how cargoes move, with some designated vessels relying on an additional ship-to-ship (STS) transfer to get oil to its final destination.

articles.title: Shipping may not return to previous operating environment: CMES
articles.summary: Shipping companies must prepare for lasting changes in trade and security patterns rather than wait for previous operating conditions to return, Wang Yongxin, president of state-controlled China Merchants Energy Shipping, said. Geopolitics, trade relationships, energy systems and supply chains are being reshaped,...
articles.body: Shipping may not return to previous operating environment: CMES in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 Shipping companies must prepare for lasting changes in trade and security patterns rather than wait for previous operating conditions to return, Wang Yongxin, president of state-controlled China Merchants Energy Shipping, said. Geopolitics, trade relationships, energy systems and supply chains are being reshaped, meaning the industry may not return to its former operating environment even if some risks ease, Wang told the Xinde Marine Forum in Hong Kong. “Many of today’s changes may not be temporary,” he said. “Rather than waiting for that environment to return, companies must make adaptability and continuity of service part of the long-term management.” Wang’s comments followed executives’ warnings during Hong Kong Maritime Week 2026 that a return to past confidence in safe passage might be difficult. Inexpensive weapons posed a continuing threat to maritime chokepoints, said Lloyd’s Register CEO Nick Brown at the Hong Kong Global Maritime Trade Summit Nov. 16 Brown noted that it was too early to determine how the conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel would be resolved. “With the way that cheap disposable weapons, if you like, single-use weapons can be deployed across chokepoints at sea, I think it’s very hard for us to see how we can all be as relaxed as we were in the previous 40 years,” Brown said. Oil and energy flows through Hormuz have recovered from their second-quarter lows but remain below prewar levels. In the week to Nov. 10, total Middle East crude exports slipped back to about 76% of their prewar levels amid persistent maritime attacks.(opens in a new tab) The seven-day moving averages for combined crude shipments from the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and Red Sea ports fell to 14.1 million barrels/day in the week to Nov. 10 from 17.3 million b/d a week earlier and a peak of 18.63 million b/d Nov. 4, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data. Total oil shipments through the strait averaged 9.1 million b/d in the third quarter, up from 5.1 million b/d in Q2 but down from 21.6 million b/d in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the US Energy Information Administration’s November energy-security data. Operational adjustments Efficiency, vessel utilization and cost control are important, but customers increasingly expected reliable services even when supply chains were disrupted, Wang said. “This year, as tanker markets and energy trade have shifted, we have adjusted fleet deployment to match customer needs, route conditions and cargo flows, while maintaining flexibility,” he said. The company said earlier that(opens in a new tab) it had deployed most of its tanker capacity outside the Strait of Hormuz as ship-to-ship transfer volumes increased. The tanker fleet had secured employment for about two-thirds of its Q4 operating days and some operating days in 2027, at freight rates substantially above those achieved in January-September. Platts Dirty Tanker Basis Global Index VLCC (Non-Scrubber Fitted Non-Eco) averaged $1,091,963/day in October, up from September’s $823,285/d and August’s average of $416,840/d. Platts is part of S&P Global Energy. Platts assessed the index at $814,585/d Nov. 17, up $14,686/d from the day prior. Specifically for the Ras Tanura-Ningbo route, the time charter equivalent earnings for non-scrubber, non-eco VLCCs stood at $1,093,541/day Nov. 17. Shipping as critical infrastructure Brown said resilient voyages required cooperation between governments, navies and commercial shipping, alongside efforts to strengthen ships and crews. “We need more governments globally to see our industry as critical infrastructure, in the same way that power stations and grids are seen as critical infrastructure,” he said. For shipowners, Wang said uncertainty also required investment decisions that could withstand different outcomes for trade, fuels and regulation. “Long-term investment cannot be based on just one version of a future,” he said. “A vessel may operate for 20 years or more, while future fuel pathways, trade patterns and regulations remain uncertain.” CMES’ diversification across tanker, dry bulk, LNG, vehicle and container shipping helped it serve different industries and navigate market cycles, Wang said. “So we ask ourselves not only which future is most likely, but also if the future turns out differently from what we expect, will we have the flexibility to adapt?” Source: Platts 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Hafnia Limited Announces Third Quarter Net Profit Of USD 170.8 million
articles.summary: Hafnia Limited, a leading product tanker company with a diversified and modern fleet of over 100 vessels, announced results for the three and nine months ended 30 September 2026. Highlights and Recent Activity Third Quarter 2026 • Recorded net profit of USD 170.8 million or USD 0.34 per share1 compared to USD 91.5...
articles.body: Hafnia Limited Announces Third Quarter Net Profit Of USD 170.8 million in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 Hafnia Limited, a leading product tanker company with a diversified and modern fleet of over 100 vessels, announced results for the three and nine months ended 30 September 2026. Highlights and Recent Activity Third Quarter 2026 • Recorded net profit of USD 170.8 million or USD 0.34 per share1 compared to USD 91.5 million or USD 0.18 per share in Q3 2025. • Fee-based businesses generated earnings of USD 6.3 million2 compared to USD 7.1 million in Q3 2025. • Time Charter Equivalent (TCE)3 earnings were USD 277.5 million compared to USD 247.0 million in Q3 2025, resulting in an average TCE3 of USD 32,708 per day. • Adjusted EBITDA3 of USD 209.7 million compared to USD 150.5 million in Q3 2025. • 74% of total earning days of the fleet were covered for Q4 2026 at USD 55,148 per day as of 13 November 2026. • Net asset value (NAV)5 was approximately USD 5.2 billion, or approximately USD 9.80 per share (NOK 94.16), at quarter end. Year-to-Date 30 September 2026 • Recorded net profit of USD 628.3 million or USD 1.26 per share1 compared to USD 230.0 million or USD 0.46 per share in YTD 9M 2025. • Fee-based businesses generated earnings of USD 22.9 million2 compared to USD 22.9 million in YTD 9M 2025. • Time Charter Equivalent (TCE)3 earnings were USD 932.9 million compared to USD 696.9 million in YTD 9M 2025, resulting in an average TCE3 of USD 36,298 per day4. • Adjusted EBITDA3 of USD 695.7 million compared to USD 409.7 million in YTD 9M 2025. • TCE per operating day is calculated as TCE income adjusted for the gains and losses recognized on the Forward Freight Agreements (FFAs), divided by available operating days. Søren Steenberg Jensen, CEO of Hafnia, commented: This is my first quarterly letter as CEO of Hafnia. I have been part of building this company since its beginnings in 2010, and I took over a business with a clear strategy, a strong balance sheet, and an experienced team at sea and ashore. My role now is to build on these strong foundations and take the company further. I want to thank our former CEO Mikael Skov for 16 years of leadership, and our seafarers and onshore colleagues for their ongoing efforts, particularly through a demanding geopolitical period. More than six months after the conflict in the Persian Gulf began, the market is still far from normal. Crude tankers have taken most of the market uplift. Their exceptional earnings pulled more LR2 vessels into dirty trades, which reduces the effective capacity of the clean fleet. Diesel markets are tight, inventories are low, and refinery runs are set to rise from their seasonal low in October. Heading into the winter market, the product tanker market is very strong. Against this backdrop, Hafnia delivered a net profit of USD 170.8 million in Q3 2026, bringing our year-to-date profit to USD 628.3 million. Our fee-based business generated USD 6.3 million. Scheduled drydockings resulted in approximately 259 off-hire days in the quarter, and we expect approximately 99 off-hire days in Q4. Our average fleet TCE1 for Q3 was USD 32,708 per day. As of 13 November 2026, 74% of our Q4 earning days are covered at an average of USD 55,148 per day. That supports a strong end to the year. At the end of the third quarter, our net asset value (NAV2) rose to approximately USD 5.2 billion, up USD 0.8 billion from Q2 2026. This is equivalent to USD 9.80 (~NOK 94.16) per share. Higher vessel values across all segments amid a strong market and a higher value for our investment in TORM have driven the increase. Our net Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio fell further to 11.9% at the end of the quarter, primarily reflecting strong operational cash flow generation and proceeds from our recent equity raise. We remain strong believers in industry consolidation. However, our approaches to TORM have not been reciprocated, and we believe continued resistance and the passage of time would erode the benefits we had hoped to deliver for shareholders. We will therefore pursue other growth and consolidation opportunities to deliver value to our shareholders. In the coming quarters, we plan to exercise eight purchase options totaling approximately USD 235 million, adding the vessels to our owned fleet at prices well below their current market value. The investment in TORM has been financially successful, and after careful consideration of our options, the Board has determined that it would be best to exit our investment in TORM, preferably through a distribution to our shareholders of all our TORM shares as a special dividend. The value of such a distribution would be well in excess of the maximum dividend distribution contemplated by our dividend policy and would also satisfy our dividend obligations for both Q3 and Q4 2026. If successfully completed, this distribution would pass the value of our TORM shares directly to shareholders and let each shareholder decide whether to hold or sell. Based on TORM’s closing share price of USD 33.73 on November 17, 2026, the special dividend would have a total value of approximately USD 686.6 million, or USD 1.2826 per Hafnia share. Hafnia would distribute 1 TORM share for every 26.3 Hafnia shares held, equivalent to 0.0380 TORM shares per Hafnia share. Entitlements that do not add up to a whole TORM share would be paid equivalent in cash, currently at USD 1.2826 for each Hafnia share they relate to. The special dividend would replace our cash dividends for Q3 and Q4 2026. The ratio would be fixed in shares, not dollars, and there would be no adjustment if the TORM share price moves before payment. Upon completion, the distribution would reduce Hafnia’s NAV by approximately USD 1.28 per share. For more information, please see our separate announcement regarding the Company’s plans for the potential special dividend. Our ability to make such a distribution depends on cooperation from third parties. If we are unable to obtain that cooperation by November 25, 2026, we intend to declare and pay a cash dividend for the quarter of 90% of net profit, in accordance with our dividend policy. We expect to announce the distribution, along with the dividend record date, no later than November 25, 2026. After Q1 2027, dividends will follow our adjusted dividend policy, under which we will pay out 100% of net profits as dividends when our net LTV is below 10%, and 90% when our net LTV is 10% or higher but below 20%. From a standing start in 2010, Hafnia has grown into one of the world’s largest product tanker companies through disciplined capital allocation. While the geopolitical and economic outlook remains uncertain, our scale and experienced team give us a solid foundation for the period ahead. Fleet1 At the end of the quarter, Hafnia’s fleet consisted of 101 owned vessels2 and 11 time chartered-in vessels. The Group’s total fleet includes 10 LR2s, 28 LR1s (including two bareboat-chartered in and two time-chartered in), 54 MRs of which 13 are IMO II (including nine time-chartered in), and 20 Handy vessels of which 18 are IMO II (including one bareboat-chartered in). The average estimated broker value of the owned fleet1 was USD 4,521 million, of which USD 4,000 million relates to Hafnia’s 100% owned fleet, and USD 521 million relates to Hafnia’s 50% share in the joint venture fleet. Including Hafnia’s 50% share in the joint venture fleet, the LR2 fleet had a broker value of USD 751 million3, the LR1 fleet had a broker value of USD 1,270 million3, the MR fleet had a broker value of USD 1,759 million4 and the Handy fleet had a broker value of USD 741 million5. The unencumbered vessels had a broker value of USD 1,104 million. The chartered-in fleet had a right-of-use asset book value of USD 76.4 million with a corresponding lease liability of USD 75.6 million. Market Review & Outlook Market Fundamentals The third quarter saw a steady but uneven recovery in Middle East oil flows after the severe disruption of the second quarter. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global oil supply rose by 2.3 million barrels per day (mb/d) month-on-month to 105.4 mb/d in October, driven by Gulf producers. Crude exports from the region increased sharply, and flows through the Strait of Hormuz grew by 0.4 mb/d to 11.8 mb/d. Ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman helped lift these flows. In those transfers, cargoes shuttled through the Strait are moved onto other tankers for onward delivery. These inefficiencies have contributed to exceptional crude tanker rates. The dislocation has also tightened product markets, particularly diesel. Although refined product exports from the Middle East recovered to 2.6 mb/d in October, highest level since the conflict began, they remain 44% below February levels. Diesel inventories fell at a time when they would normally build, ahead of autumn refinery maintenance and peak winter demand. Middle East net diesel exports in October were 0.8 mb/d lower year-on-year and Russian exports were down by 0.4 mb/d, only partly offset by higher supply from other sources. For product tankers, the effect is mixed but increasingly supportive. In our view, lower exports from Russia and the Middle East have shifted sourcing to alternative suppliers, lengthening some trade routes and adding tonne-miles. Inventories are also low, with global oil stocks being observed at 462 mb below end-of February levels at the end of October. Forward View The outlook remains highly uncertain and depends on security in the Strait of Hormuz and the pace of recovery in Middle Eastern product exports. The recent escalation in attacks on regional energy infrastructure and tanker traffic threatens further gains, and damage to refineries continues to hold back product exports. High prices and a weaker economic outlook are also weighing on demand, particularly for diesel. The IEA now forecasts global oil demand to fall by 2.7 mb/d in 2026 and recover by 2.0 mb/d in 2027, leaving consumption 0.6% below 2025 levels. Inventories, however, remain supportive of seaborne trade. Global refinery runs are forecast to rise from a seasonal low of 81.3 mb/d in October to 84.7 mb/d by year-end. IEA member countries have also backed faster emergency stock releases, with priority on diesel. In our view, rebuilding depleted strategic and commercial stocks should add further cargo demand, although the transition may be volatile. For 2027, the IEA expects global oil supply to rise by 6.6 mb/d, well ahead of demand, as OPEC+ production recovers and non-OPEC+ output keeps growing. This would allow inventories to be rebuilt, but only if Gulf flows recover sustainably and the security situation stabilizes. Tanker demand depends heavily on geopolitics, but the supply side is more predictable, and our view is unchanged. With crude tanker earnings at exceptional levels, more LR2s are moving into the Aframax trade. This reduces effective supply in the product tanker market and could also limit the net growth in clean-trading capacity from the existing orderbook, as we believe this migration pattern will continue. While any easing of OFAC sanctions could bring some tonnage back into the mainstream market, we expect the impact to be limited. A significant share of OFAC-sanctioned tankers remains subject to UK or EU sanctions, limiting their access to certain trades. Furthermore, the relatively advanced age of these vessels could delay their return to mainstream trading, given potential maintenance, inspection, insurance, and commercial requirements. Dividend Information The board has not declared a dividend for the quarter yet. We believe it would be beneficial to our shareholders to distribute the 20,356,061 shares of TORM we own as a special dividend. Our ability to make such a distribution, however, depends on cooperation from third parties, which is beyond our control. If we are unable to obtain that cooperation by November 25, 2026, we intend to declare and pay a cash dividend for the quarter of 90% of net profit, in accordance with our dividend policy. We expect to announce whether we will declare the special dividend through a distribution of the TORM shares or through a cash dividend in accordance with our existing dividend policy, along with the dividend record date, no later than November 25, 2026. Full Report Source: Hafnia 2026-11-19 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: ENGINE: Europe & Africa Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook in International Shipping News 19/11/2026 Northwest Europe Prompt fuel availability is tight in ARA ports, with buyers recommended lead times of 5-7 days to get good coverage from suppliers, a trader told ENGINE. The ARA’s independently held fuel oil stocks have averaged 6% higher so far in November than in October, according to Insights Global data. The region’s independent gasoil inventories – which include diesel and heating oil – have risen by 1% so far in November compared with October, according to Insights Global data. Fuel availability is normal in Hamburg, and buyers need to book at least five days ahead, a trader told ENGINE. Buyers are advised to enquire around 10 days ahead for supplies off Denmark’s Skaw and in Sweden’s Gothenburg, a trader said. Mediterranean Fuel availability is tight for prompt delivery dates in Gibraltar Strait ports, a trader said. Lead times of 6-7 days are recommended to secure deliveries at competitive prices, the trader added. ULSFO availability is very tight in Gibraltar and Algeciras, the trader added. The weather is expected to be rough until Thursday evening in Gibraltar and Algeciras, with winds forecast to exceed 25 knots. Gibraltar is seeing some congestion. Around 16 vessels queued for bunkering in the port on Wednesday morning, port agent MH Bland said. Some suppliers were running 16-24 hours late on deliveries, while other suppliers were delayed more than that, the port agent added. In neighbouring Algeciras, some suppliers are delayed by up to 18 hours, MH Bland said. Barge supplies in Ceuta are delayed by 4-6 hours, according to the port agent. Fuel availability is tight in Las Palmas, with buyers advised lead times of around 7-10 days for most deliveries, a trader told ENGINE. In Barcelona, bunker supplies need a notice of 4-5 days, according to a trader. Fuel availability is stable off Malta, and buyers are recommended to book around 4-5 days ahead to secure supplies with low premiums, a trader told ENGINE. In the Greek port of Piraeus, fuel availability is tight for prompt supplies. Some suppliers can deliver with a week of lead time or more, a trader said. In Turkey’s Istanbul, rough weather with south-westerly winds of more than 30 knots has suspended all bunker operations, a trader told ENGINE. Conditions are expected to improve by Friday evening or Saturday morning. Africa In Senegal’s Dakar, VLSFO and LSMGO availability is tight for prompt supplies, with deliveries available from 25-26 November, a supplier told ENGINE. In Togo’s Lome, VLSFO and LSMGO availability is tight for prompt supplies. Buyers are advised to enquire at least seven days ahead of deliveries, a trader said. VLSFO bunker availability is tight for prompt dates at the Lagos anchorage, and buyers are recommended lead times of 4-9 days, a local supplier told ENGINE. VLSFO is unavailable at Angola’s Luanda anchorage, while LSMGO supplies need 4-5 days, a supplier said. Off Namibia’s Walvis Bay, fuel availability is tight for prompt supplies. Some suppliers are quoting their earliest delivery dates from 23-24 November, a trader told ENGINE. Fuel availability has improved in South Africa’s Durban, but remains tight for prompt deliveries. Buyers are advised lead times of 5-7 days, a trader said. Fuel availability is tight for prompt supplies in Port Louis, with buyers recommended lead times of around 5-7 days, a trader noted. Prompt bunker availability is tight in Mozambique’s Nacala and Maputo, with buyers advised lead times of 5-7 days for most supplies, a trader said. articles.body: Steer Acquires Mercator International Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 © Steer Steer has completed the acquisition of Mercator International, a specialist ports, maritime and freight consultancy, as it continues to expand its international advisory business. Headquartered in Kirkland, Washington, Mercator provides strategic, commercial and transaction advice to investors, port authorities, terminal operators, ocean carriers and logistics businesses. Led by Steve Rothberg, Mike Petro and Derik Andreoli, the firm has completed more than 150 commercial due diligence projects and advised over 40 investors and financial institutions on transactions worldwide since its founding in 2000. Mercator is Steer’s fourth acquisition since 2021, alongside Fourth Economy in the US and Amberside Advisors and Evolution Infrastructure in the UK. Mercator becomes part of Steer’s North America division, led by Herb Higginbotham, and will continue to operate under the Mercator name, with complete continuity for its clients and current projects. The combination brings Mercator’s commercial and operational expertise together with Steer’s wider transportation and infrastructure capabilities, including rail, freight, infrastructure planning and investment advisory. Mercator’s experience includes advising the Ports of Seattle and Tacoma on the formation of the Northwest Seaport Alliance, the Quebec Port Authority on a new container terminal, and the consortium led by Macquarie on its acquisition of Long Beach Container Terminal. Mercator will work closely with Steer’s ports and maritime practice, led by Alberto Preti in Italy and Steve Wray in the UK. Coming after Wray’s appointment from Infrata earlier this year, the acquisition reflects Steer’s continued commitment to the sector as it builds its share of the global infrastructure transactions market.

articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: BNMK 0819/Shutterstock Nine major shipping associations are urging governments to reach an agreement on global greenhouse gas regulations, warning that continued uncertainty threatens investment in cleaner ships and alternative fuels ahead of critical negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). The joint statement , issued Wednesday, calls for practical, enforceable and globally consistent rules that would give shipowners and fuel suppliers the certainty needed to invest in maritime decarbonization. The appeal comes as governments prepare to revisit the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, whose formal adoption was postponed in October 2025 amid opposition from the United States and several oil-producing countries. The framework, approved in draft form in April 2025, would combine progressively stricter greenhouse gas fuel-intensity requirements with a mechanism that places a price on certain emissions. The nine organizations—including BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), INTERTANKO, INTERCARGO and the World Shipping Council (WSC)—reaffirmed their support for the IMO’s goal of achieving net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. However, they stressed that any agreement must account for the cost and availability of alternative fuels, provide flexible compliance mechanisms and avoid overlapping national and regional regulations. The statement stops short of explicitly endorsing the existing Net-Zero Framework in its current form, instead acknowledging that alternative government proposals remain under consideration. Industry Support Comes With Conditions The appeal follows a recent analysis by InfluenceMap that found broad industry support for a global IMO climate agreement, but significant differences over carbon pricing, fuel standards and how emissions from alternative fuels should be calculated. The London-based research organization found that industry support has become more cautious since the framework’s adoption was postponed last year. Before that decision, ICS and WSC had backed the proposed framework as is. More recently, shipping associations have emphasized reaching an agreement without explicitly endorsing the original package. Another point of contention is the relationship between global IMO rules and existing European regulations. Several shipping associations have called for reviewing or harmonizing the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime requirements once an international framework is established, arguing that overlapping regulations would impose unnecessary costs. Critical Negotiations Ahead The renewed industry push comes ahead of an IMO working group meeting November 23–27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s MEPC 85 session from November 30 to December 3. A previously adjourned extraordinary session could resume December 4 to consider adoption of the framework. Negotiators face deep divisions over carbon pricing, compliance costs and the treatment of different marine fuels. For shipowners making investment decisions on vessels expected to operate for decades, the outcome could shape everything from ship design to fuel procurement and infrastructure development. The industry groups say a global agreement is essential to maintaining a level playing field. Whether governments can deliver that certainty while preserving the emissions-reduction ambitions of the original framework remains an open question. articles.body: Rhenus Group is merging Langarri Logistica and Transportes Frigoríficos Ramón Villalba, bringing their road freight operations in Spain under a single corporate structure and the Rhenus brand. Both companies are already part of the group. The merger combines their complementary transport activities within Rhenus’ Overland Division in Spain while maintaining their existing services and geographical coverage. Langarri Logistica, which joined Rhenus in 2019, specialises in regional parcel distribution, pallet transport and business-to-business deliveries across northern Spain. Based in Gipuzkoa, the company has expanded its network through facilities in Elgoibar, Cantabria, Santander, Logroño and Burgos. Its operations also include connections with France. Meanwhile, Barcelona-based Transportes Frigoríficos Ramón Villalba has been part of Rhenus since 2017. The company specialises in refrigerated transport, general cargo and freight services between mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands. Its activities include the transportation of dry, fresh and frozen food products, alongside groupage and full-load services. Rhenus consolidates Spanish road freight operations The merger brings both companies’ regional expertise and established customer relationships into a unified organisation. According to Rhenus, customers will continue to receive the same transport services and geographical coverage under the group’s common brand. “Both companies have built their businesses over many years through a deep understanding of their markets and close relationships with their customers,” said Javier Berenguer, Managing Director of the Overland Division of Rhenus in Spain. “Preserving that knowledge and entrepreneurial spirit is essential as we look ahead,” Berenguer added. The integration forms part of Rhenus’ efforts to consolidate its road freight activities in Spain and connect regional operations more closely with its wider international logistics network.

articles.title: Geneva Dry: TCC’s Emily Koo on the disconnect between dry bulk rates and asset prices
articles.summary: TCC Group’s Emily Koo warns that elevated vessel prices, an overreliance on market statistics and a narrow focus on technology risk distracting dry bulk shipping from the bigger challenges ahead. The growing disconnect between freight rates and vessel prices, and the industry’s tendency to overlook what might go...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Greater China Maritime CEO Geneva Dry: TCC’s Emily Koo on the disconnect between dry bulk rates and asset prices Splash November 19, 2026 0 232 2 minutes read TCC Group’s Emily Koo warns that elevated vessel prices, an overreliance on market statistics and a narrow focus on technology risk distracting dry bulk shipping from the bigger challenges ahead. The growing disconnect between freight rates and vessel prices, and the industry’s tendency to overlook what might go wrong, will be among the key talking points when dry bulk executives gather in Geneva next April, reckons Emily Koo of Hong Kong shipowner TCC Group. Koo, one of more than 50 shipowners to take the stage at Geneva Dry 2027, is concerned that the industry is becoming too focused on explaining freight market rallies through statistics rather than examining the underlying health of the shipping business. She questions how long owners can continue justifying the disconnect between earnings and asset values while “sweeping what might go wrong” under the rug. With vessel prices remaining elevated, Koo believes shipowners also need to reconsider how they approach expansion. “Growth does not only mean buying a ship,” she says. There are different ways owners can position themselves for growth in these market conditions she says, citing building stronger relationships instead of going it alone, and examining whether equity should be reallocated across segments as examples. “Prohibitive pricing makes it difficult for companies to go it alone,” she says. Koo is similarly cautious about the industry’s growing enthusiasm for technology, warning that the pursuit of efficiency in individual areas of a business risks obscuring the bigger picture. “I think technology may force us to consider only a snapshot of commercial performance,” she says. While digital solutions can help optimise specific operations, Koo believes shipping must be viewed as a complete service rather than a collection of individual performance indicators. That means maintaining a consistent approach throughout an organisation, from the shipowner and management team to the seafarers delivering the service aboard vessels. Koo is group managing director and fourth-generation custodian of Hong Kong’s TCC Group, whose origins date to 1917, when her great-grandfather Koo Chung-shui established the family shipping business in Shanghai. The group subsequently relocated its operations to Hong Kong, building a century-long reputation in dry bulk and tanker shipping. Her preference for looking beyond headline numbers also shapes what she hopes to take away from Geneva Dry. Rather than presentations dominated by familiar market data, she wants to hear how industry leaders interpret the challenges facing dry bulk shipping and how they intend to respond. articles.title: Contractor appointed for port of Gothenburg fairway deepening
articles.summary: The Swedish Maritime Administration has awarded a joint venture of Boskalis Sweden AB, Van Oord Sweden AB and Rohde Nielsen A/S the contract to deepen and widen the fairway to the Port of Gothenburg. The award is an important step in the Skandia Gateway project, which will allow today’s largest container vessels to...
articles.body: The Swedish Maritime Administration has awarded a joint venture of Boskalis Sweden AB, Van Oord Sweden AB and Rohde Nielsen A/S the contract to deepen and widen the fairway to the Port of Gothenburg. The award is an important step in the Skandia Gateway project, which will allow today’s largest container vessels to be received fully laden, and even larger vessels in future. The depth of the fairway currently limits how much cargo the largest container vessels can carry to and from Gothenburg, the largest port in the Nordic region. The contract covers dredging of about 7 million cubic metres of loose material and rock and adaptation of the fairway markings, making it one of the largest dredging projects in Sweden. Fairway work is due to start in August 2027, and the whole project is expected to be complete in autumn 2028, when the port will be able to receive vessels with a draft of 16.5 metres, compared with 13.5 metres today. An option in the contract allows the port to order further deepening for drafts of up to 17.5 metres. The base contract is worth approximately SEK 2.3 billion, with the possibility of additional work through agreed options. Signing between the Swedish Maritime Administration, the Gothenburg Port Authority and the joint venture is planned for the end of 2026, provided the award is not legally challenged. After the previous procurement was cancelled in autumn 2025, the project optimised the fairway design and reduced the scope of dredging. Meanwhile quayside work has continued under the port’s management: the quay reinforcement is complete and separate dredging close to the quay is under way. Elin Dörrheide, Project Manager for Skandia Gateway at the Port of Gothenburg, said the project is progressing as planned and that rising cargo volumes, deeper-draft vessels and long-term congestion in other major European ports keep the deepening strategically vital. Thomas Nord, Head of Unit at the Swedish Maritime Administration, said the measures will let the largest container vessels carry more cargo to and from Gothenburg, strengthening access to efficient maritime transport and Sweden’s competitiveness. Jenny Röström Wicander, Project Manager at the Swedish Maritime Administration, called it a very important milestone after years of studies, environmental permitting and design optimisation.

articles.title: The missing middle in Hong Kong’s maritime workforce
articles.summary: The city wants to expand its role in global shipping, but its maritime ambitions face a stubborn recruitment problem. Finding graduates is one thing; attracting and retaining the experienced professionals needed to run an international maritime centre is quite another. Hong Kong has no shortage of ambitions for its...
articles.body: Greater China Operations The missing middle in Hong Kong’s maritime workforce Splash November 19, 2026 0 296 4 minutes read Hong Kong Cyberport Hong Kong Cyberport The city wants to expand its role in global shipping, but its maritime ambitions face a stubborn recruitment problem. Finding graduates is one thing; attracting and retaining the experienced professionals needed to run an international maritime centre is quite another. Hong Kong has no shortage of ambitions for its maritime industry. It wants to become a centre for green fuel trading, ship finance, digital technology and sophisticated fleet management. But there is one asset that cannot be imported overnight: an experienced marine superintendent who has spent years at sea and knows how to keep an increasingly complex fleet operating safely. The city’s problem is not simply persuading school-leavers to consider a career in shipping. It is attracting and retaining the people 10 or 15 years further along, when hard-won technical knowledge meets commercial judgment and when employers in Singapore, mainland China and industries far beyond shipping are competing for the same individuals. Revealing numbers The Vocational Training Council’s latest maritime manpower survey counts 25,993 employees in 2024, including non-Hong Kong seafarers, with 13,746 in shore-based jobs. It records just 384 vacancies, including 192 ashore, but a 9.1% turnover rate among shore-based staff. A low snapshot vacancy rate does not mean companies can easily find a chief engineer turned superintendent, an experienced claims handler or a specialist surveyor. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, says “talent is one of the sector’s most urgent execution challenges”. Hong Kong needs not just new graduates, he argues, but professionals who can move from seagoing and technical roles into commercial and leadership positions. Earlier VTC research identified a hollowed-out middle in high-value maritime services, with senior staff nearing retirement and junior employees still acquiring experience. It also identified a shortage of people with seagoing qualifications for jobs such as port captain, technical superintendent and ship surveyor. Even the Marine Department has struggled to fill its specialist positions. At classification society RINA, the shortage is practical rather than theoretical. Brian Yam, its commercial director for Hong Kong and Taiwan, says one particular difficulty is hiring experienced ship surveyors locally. Local pathways into naval architecture and marine engineering are limited, and relatively few Hong Kong youngsters spend the years at sea needed to acquire the qualifications and experience employers want. Career ladders There is a fundamental timing problem. A short course can teach a new regulation; it cannot produce the judgment gained from an engine-room failure, a drydocking or years of managing crews and contractors. Shipmanagers are responding by building their own career ladders. Anglo-Eastern chief executive Bjorn Hojgaard says five members of the company’s executive management team started their careers at sea and approximately 75% of its shore managers have been promoted from its seagoing workforce. “Mid-career is the point where many professionals weigh a move into adjacent sectors,” he says. Employers must offer progression, mentoring and competitive rewards before valuable experience walks out of the maritime sector altogether. Quality of life Hong Kong is also competing on quality of life. Housing costs, education, family considerations and alternative careers in finance, technology and family offices affect whether a specialist accepts a posting or stays for the long term. Tax concessions for maritime businesses are of limited use if they create additional corporate structures without bringing experienced decision-makers and their families to the city. Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group, makes a revealing point about the labour market. At mid-career, people make decisions based on “career optionality — having 10 potential employers rather than two”. An attractive maritime centre therefore needs competing companies, not merely a few very large ones. Recruitment becomes easier when changing jobs does not also mean changing countries. Insurance faces much the same challenge. Deborah Yu, regional director for Asia at London P&I, says: “Mid-career professionals are mobile and have attractive opportunities in many other regional hubs.” Underwriters, claims handlers and specialist surveyors need both competitive remuneration and credible prospects of advancement. The technical requirements are changing, too. Methanol and ammonia, cyber security, emissions verification, remote monitoring and AI are creating new jobs while changing established ones. Ioannis Stefanou, managing director of shipmanagement at Wallem Group, says the competition for skilled professionals extends far beyond shipping. The industry needs to show younger recruits that maritime careers are global, technologically advanced and connected to decarbonisation rather than simply selling a lifetime of paperwork and port calls. Progress There are signs of action. The Hong Kong Shipowners Association launched its academy earlier this month, building on a 16-organisation Maritime Talent Cultivation Alliance established last year. The academy is intended to upgrade members’ knowledge and skills, not simply introduce schoolchildren to the industry. The government’s September policy address also proposed a maritime academy and an institution-enterprise training model with clearer cross-disciplinary career pathways. Training already has tangible public backing. Hong Kong pays eligible deck and engineer cadets HK$10,000 a month during qualifying sea service, and its maritime training fund supports further professional courses and examinations. In April, the government and industry partners organised a train-the-trainer programme on green marine fuels, recognising that new bunkering infrastructure is of little value without people who know how to use it safely. Hext says maritime careers must become “more visible, portable and future-facing”. Structured internships, recognised sea-to-shore qualifications and mid-career transfers could help turn isolated training programmes into genuine progression routes. The next test is not how many academies open or how many students attend a career fair. It is how many surveyors, fleet managers, brokers, claims specialists and marine engineers actually take posts in Hong Kong, and how many remain five years later. The city can fund a ship, register it and insure it. Keeping the know-how needed to operate all three businesses may be the more demanding investment. (Screenshot from video) The LPG tanker TARA GAS remained on fire and adrift in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, according to a new navigational warning, as independently verified video showed the vessel engulfed in a massive blaze following repeated attacks that left one seafarer missing. The latest developments come as ADNOC Logistics & Services confirmed a separate attack on one of its tankers in the waterway, leaving another crew member missing and 11 injured. A NAVAREA IX navigational warning issued at 1500 UTC Wednesday identified TARA GAS as still burning and drifting southeast, approximately 5.7 nautical miles off Khawr Ghub Ali, Oman. Mariners were cautioned to avoid the disabled vessel. The warning provides the clearest indication yet that the fire continued into Wednesday, despite some reports suggesting it had been extinguished. Meanwhile, Reuters has independently verified dramatic footage circulating on social media showing TARA GAS engulfed in flames, with thick black smoke billowing above the vessel. The news agency confirmed the location using coastal landmarks, satellite imagery and topographical data, while matching the vessel’s superstructure and stern to archival photographs. NASA satellite fire-detection data also recorded thermal activity at the location on November 17. Reuters could not establish exactly when the footage was recorded. The Panama-flagged LPG tanker was initially attacked on November 16, approximately seven nautical miles north of Khasab, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) . The strike disabled the vessel and caused an engine-room fire. A subsequent attack on November 17 sparked another fire and forced the crew to abandon ship. Omani authorities rescued 24 of the vessel’s 25 crew members, while one Indian seafarer remains missing. India’s Ministry of External Affairs said two Indian crew members were hospitalized in Khasab. The attacks and rescue operations were detailed in gCaptain’s earlier reporting . In another significant development, ADNOC Logistics & Services confirmed Wednesday that one of its vessels was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on the evening of November 17. The company said one crew member remained unaccounted for, while the remaining crew had been evacuated. Eleven seafarers sustained injuries and were receiving medical care where required. “Our immediate priority is supporting the search and rescue effort, our crew and those affected,” ADNOC L&S said. The company did not identify the vessel. However, maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified it as the Liberian-flagged product tanker NAVIG8 MESSI , which is commercially managed by ADNOC L&S. A new time-late report from the UKMTO appears to correspond to the ADNOC incident. The report, based on information from local authorities, said a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile approximately 13 nautical miles north of Khasab on November 17. A fire broke out aboard the vessel but was subsequently extinguished. UKMTO said search-and-rescue efforts were continuing for one missing crew member, while the extent of the vessel’s damage and any environmental impact remained unknown. The warning did not identify the tanker by name. The reported attack on NAVIG8 MESSI would be the second against the vessel in recent months. ADNOC previously confirmed that two of its ships were targeted by drones in the Strait of Hormuz on August 13, with Vanguard identifying them as NAVIG8 MESSI and TARIF . No injuries were reported in those earlier incidents. The latest attacks underscore the continuing danger to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The development follows the completion of ONE’s acquisition of Pantos Holdings’ entire equity interest in Pan Hai An. Following the transaction, Hai An holds a 51% stake in Pan Hai An, while ONE owns the remaining 49%. The parties completed the relevant legal procedures in August 2026. These included amendments to the company’s Investment Registration Certificate and Enterprise Registration Certificate. The Hai Phong Economic Zone Authority and the Hai Phong Department of Finance approved the changes. Pan Hai An launches VSX service Following the completion of the transaction, Pan Hai An launched its first international container shipping service. The new VSX service connects Vietnam with Singapore, Hong Kong and Qinzhou in China’s Guangxi region through regular sailings. Two chartered container ships operate the service: HAIAN VIEW and HAIAN DELL. Each vessel has a capacity of 1,577 TEU. The launch marks Pan Hai An’s expansion beyond its established warehousing and container depot activities into regional liner shipping. Hai An expects the partnership to provide access to ONE’s international customer base and global shipping network. The Vietnamese company said the cooperation could also support further development in the Intra-Asia market. It may eventually create opportunities for the partners to explore intercontinental shipping services.
