November 18, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Sunshine Seeds Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, according to estimates from two industry sources, as Kyiv ramps up strikes on energy infrastructure. Russia is already facing domestic fuel shortages in some regions and restricted ex port capacity due to crippling Ukrainian strikes on port s. Reduced refining could also tighten global fuel markets and hamper Russia's ability to deliver on a deal to ex port diesel to the United States. The attacks now have disrupted or halted operations at 15 of Russia's 35 major refineries, the two people said, up from 9 in the middle of last week. Russia's energy ministry did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. MOSCOW AND KYIV RAMPING UP STRIKES ON ENERGY TARGETS US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on October 11. Though neither Moscow nor Kyiv acknowledged agreeing to it and attacks continued, Ukrainian strikes did ease for roughly two weeks. The war has since intensified, however, with Ukrainian drone attacks increasing in scale and frequency as Russia ramps up its own drone and missile strikes. Ukraine hit a strategically im port ant bridge and targeted oil refineries this week in what Russian ‌defence ministry data showed on Monday was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of the war in 2022. Following near-daily drone strikes over the last 20 days, crude processing volumes at Russian refineries have fallen to around 400,000 metric tons per day, or around 3 million barrels per day, from over 700,000 metric tons per day at the end of October, the estimates showed. The combined nominal capacity of Russian refineries affected by the attacks since late October stands at around 500,000 tons per day, equivalent to approximately 54% of the country's total primary refining capacity of an estimated 930,000 tons per day. However, the sources said that, given the gradual reduction in operating capacity, average crude processing volumes in November remain above 500,000 tons per day, about 5% to 10% below September and October levels. Major Russian refineries affected by the attacks include plants in Ryazan, Yaroslavl, Kirishi and the Volga region, the people said. (Reuters)

Join the leading maritime news network File Photo: Igor Grochev / Shutterstock (Bloomberg) — More liquefied natural gas vessels have diverted toward Europe in recent days, bolstering supplies in a tight market and pressuring prices. At least two tankers carrying US LNG have rerouted recently away from Egypt in the Mediterranean Sea, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg and intelligence firm Kpler. That’s in addition to two ships laden with US fuel that turned sharply north toward Europe, diverting away from Asia, since last week. The diversions come amid weaker demand from some major buyers in Asia — where LNG prices have fetched a discount to Europe — and other regions, although global supplies remain tight because of continued disruptions in the Middle East. The LNG flows to Europe have helped curb prices there, after benchmark gas futures hit an almost four-year high last month. Read More: European Gas Slips as Steady Supply Tempers Mideast Worries Despite persistent shipping risks in the Strait of Hormuz, there has been an uptick in flows from LNG giant Qatar, and less competition between Asia and Europe for cargoes, Kpler principal gas and LNG analyst Ronald Pinto said. For Egypt, the recent price rallies made spot LNG purchases more expensive, and there have also been some capacity expansions scheduled to increase gas flows from Israel to Egypt, he said. Egypt’s cabinet earlier this month approved a rationing plan for power consumption that state bodies will implement during the current financial year to cope with the spillover effects of the Iran war. Egypt had to curb some electricity usage this year as it grappled with high fuel costs due to the conflict. The Al Qassar tanker, carrying US LNG, turned west away from Egypt earlier this week after reaching the country’s Port Said, according to ship-tracking data. Kpler estimates it’s now heading toward Europe. The Amaryllis Knutsen vessel, also loaded with US fuel, made a sharp U-turn on Tuesday near Egypt. Separately, there’s been a diversion from Egypt toward Asia recently, based on Kpler and data on Bloomberg, with the Greenergy Wind tanker turning south in the mid-Atlantic on Tuesday. It’s signaling the Cape of Good Hope, a usual route toward Asia. A sustained fall in LNG spot prices could prompt buyers in South and Southeast Asia to purchase more cargoes, especially as big importers remain on the sidelines, according to traders. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: US Cracks Down on Iran Oil Blockade, Threatening Action
articles.summary: The US military will treat ships that receive cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran as attempting to evade its blockade of Iranian ports and could take action against them, according to an advisory issued by US Central Command (CENTCOM) on…
articles.body: US Cracks Down on Iran Oil Blockade, Threatening Action Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 © Adobe Stock/alones The US military will treat ships that receive cargo at sea from vessels loaded in Iran as attempting to evade its blockade of Iranian ports and could take action against them, according to an advisory issued by US Central Command (CENTCOM) on Wednesday. The US naval blockade on Iran-related oil exports was first imposed on April 13 and lifted in June after Washington reached a draft understanding with Tehran. It was reimposed on July 14 after the agreement collapsed. "Any ship that receives cargo via a ship-to-ship transfer with a vessel subject to the blockade and carrying cargo loaded at an Iranian port or coastline may be considered to be evading the blockade, even if it has not entered Iranian ports or the Iranian coastline," CENTCOM said in an update. "Such ships may be stopped, boarded, diverted, captured, or directed to proceed to the Iranian port where the cargo originated." Ships that fail to comply immediately with lawful orders from blockade or boarding forces could face enforcement action, "including the use of force consistent with applicable law", the advisory added. Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite the US naval blockade, according to shipping intelligence and security sources who spoke to Reuters in October. Iran's crude exports, however, have remained near a standstill for months, shipping sources say. (Reuters)

articles.summary: A Houston ship pilot has been indicted on a federal seaman’s manslaughter charge over a deadly 2024 collision in the Houston Ship Channel, in what federal officials describe as the...

The towboat rolled to starboard after being struck and later capsized and sank, killing one crewmember. (Source: NTSB/U.S. Coast Guard) A Houston ship pilot has been indicted on a federal seaman’s manslaughter charge over a deadly 2024 collision in the Houston Ship Channel, in what federal officials describe as the first prosecution of its kind involving a ship pilot. Darris Ornel Jefferson, 39, is accused of misconduct, negligence and inattention to his duties while piloting the bulk carrier Yangze 7 on July 19, 2024, when it collided with the towing vessel Miss Peggy near Lynchburg, Texas, according to the U.S. Department of Justice . The Miss Peggy capsized and sank with five crewmembers aboard. Four were rescued, while a fifth, identified in court records as 25-year-old deckhand Aquarius Lowman, was later found dead in the wreckage. One surviving crewmember suffered serious injuries and another sustained minor injuries. The indictment follows a National Transportation Safety Board investigation released in August that found the pilot had been distracted by an extended, nonoperational cellphone conversation with another pilot while navigating the busy waterway. Investigators determined that the call lasted 39 minutes and ended just two minutes and 16 seconds before the collision. The distraction contributed to the pilot’s failure to detect the Miss Peggy ahead of the bulk carrier. The NTSB also identified failures elsewhere on the vessels. The Yangze 7 bridge team did not detect the towboat until it was less than a ship’s length ahead, while the Miss Peggy captain failed to detect the bulk carrier approaching from astern. Investigators concluded that the collision resulted from a loss of situational awareness by the pilot, the bulk carrier’s bridge team and the towboat’s captain due to failures to maintain proper lookouts. The investigation also found that the Houston Pilots organization had no policy at the time prohibiting nonoperational use of personal electronic devices by pilots directing vessel movements. The NTSB subsequently recommended that the Coast Guard and American Pilots’ Association establish restrictions on such use. The American Pilots’ Association, responding to the NTSB findings in August, said the pilot’s performance had fallen short of professional standards and pledged to work with regulators to strengthen safeguards against distracted navigation. The collision caused an estimated $3.7 million in damages, salvage expenses and pollution mitigation costs, according to the NTSB. The criminal indictment now places the incident under a federal statute that allows prosecutors to pursue charges against maritime officers and others whose misconduct, negligence or inattention results in a death. If convicted, Jefferson faces up to 10 years in federal prison and a $250,000 fine. Jefferson is scheduled to make his initial appearance before U.S. Magistrate Judge Christina Bryan on November 24. The Coast Guard investigated the case, which is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Jason E. Corley. The allegations have not been proven in court, and Jefferson is presumed innocent unless convicted. ABC Affiliate WGNO via REUTERS The U.S. Coast Guard has established a temporary safety zone on the Mississippi River in New Orleans through December 11 as salvage crews prepare to recover the American Heritage river cruise ship, which capsized after being struck by a tanker last week. The temporary final rule, published Wednesday in the Federal Register, formalizes restrictions first imposed November 13 following the collision between the tanker Atlantic Asphalt and the docked American Cruise Lines vessel near the Crescent City Connection Bridge. The safety zone covers a one-mile stretch of the Lower Mississippi River between mile markers 95.5 and 96.5, extending 500 feet from the left descending bank, or east bank. Vessels and personnel are prohibited from entering the restricted area without authorization from the Captain of the Port of New Orleans. The Coast Guard said the restrictions are necessary because of potential debris in the water and hazards associated with salvage vessels, personnel and heavy equipment. Recovery operations are expected to take several weeks, although the safety zone may be canceled before December 11 if conditions permit. The zone does not amount to a monthlong shutdown of the Mississippi River. According to a November 16 update from the City of New Orleans, the alternate navigation channel remains closed, but limited two-way traffic is permitted through the main span of the Crescent City Connection Bridge. Deep-draft vessels and towing vessels pushing 10 or more barges remain restricted to one-way transit. The November 13 collision caused American Heritage to capsize alongside the pier, triggering a major rescue operation involving federal and local emergency responders and nearby commercial vessels. According to the National Transportation Safety Board, 190 passengers and crew were aboard the riverboat at the time of the accident, with 36 people hospitalized. All personnel aboard both vessels were accounted for. The NTSB is leading the investigation into the collision. A unified command comprising the Coast Guard and American Cruise Lines has been established to oversee lightering and salvage operations. Divers began inspecting the submerged vessel on November 15 to assess hull damage and help develop a recovery plan. Containment boom has also been deployed around the wreck as a precaution. New Orleans officials said Monday that an initial sheen had dissipated and no additional pollution had been observed. The Coast Guard said it will continue monitoring conditions and issue updated navigation restrictions as the salvage operation progresses. articles.summary: A potential strike at the nation’s busiest container port complex is back on the table after contract negotiations between waterfront employers and a union representing about 250 port security workers...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The shipping ports of Los Angeles (top left) and Long Beach are seen from the window of a commercial aircraft over Long Beach, California, U.S. March 13, 2023. REUTERS/Chris Helgren A potential strike at the nation’s busiest container port complex is back on the table after contract negotiations between waterfront employers and a union representing about 250 port security workers failed to produce a breakthrough. The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) warned Wednesday that members of International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 could walk off the job as early as 12:01 a.m. Saturday, November 21, when their latest contract extension expires. According to PMA, Tuesday’s negotiations ended with little progress, and the union has indicated it is unwilling to agree to another extension. The two sides are scheduled to meet again Friday, leaving little time to avert a potential disruption. Although Local 26 represents just 2% of the ILWU workforce at the ports, its members provide security at six container terminals responsible for more than half of the cargo moving through the Los Angeles-Long Beach port complex. Those terminals handle approximately 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo, according to PMA. The concern is that a strike by the watchmen could quickly spread beyond the 250 workers directly involved in the dispute. Thousands of longshore workers, marine clerks and foremen covered by separate labor agreements are expected to honor Local 26 picket lines, potentially bringing vessel operations, container movements and truck access to a halt at affected terminals. The dispute comes at a particularly sensitive time for the Southern California supply chain, with the ports handling heavy cargo volumes ahead of the holiday shopping season. A prolonged shutdown could disrupt rail and trucking operations, delay imports and exports, and create congestion extending well beyond the waterfront. Employers Detail Contract Offer PMA said its latest proposal includes a one-time $3,200 bonus for each Local 26 member and wage increases that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000. The association said the offer would also preserve fully employer-paid healthcare for active workers and retirees, which it values at more than $62,000 annually, while increasing annual pension benefits to as much as $93,200 for the longest-serving workers. PMA accused the union of making little movement on its demands despite more than a year of negotiations, including talks assisted by the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. The union’s response to the latest employer proposals was not immediately available. Local 26 members are responsible for checking identification and credentials at terminal gates, conducting security patrols and reporting safety concerns. Their previous labor agreement expired in July 2025, with workers continuing under a series of extensions. The dispute is separate from the coastwide labor agreement covering most West Coast dockworkers, which runs through 2028. Economic Stakes PMA pointed to an analysis by maritime economist John Martin estimating that the six affected terminals handled approximately 6.2 million containers in 2025 and supported nearly 4.2 million jobs nationwide through direct and indirect economic activity. The analysis attributed $885 billion in national economic activity to cargo moving through those facilities last year. That figure represents the economic activity associated with the terminals, not an estimate of losses from a potential strike. PMA warned that losses could mount rapidly if vessels are unable to discharge cargo and containers already inside the terminals cannot be moved out. articles.body: The Northwest Seaport Alliance recorded strong import volumes in October 2026, with full imports growing 13.1% compared with October 2025. The gateway attributes the result to its reliable berth window, west coast-leading low rail dwell times and cargo diverted from other ports because of ongoing congestion. Total volumes, international and domestic, reached 235,210 TEUs, up 0.5 percent year-on-year. Year-to-date volumes stand at 2,409,441 TEUs, with full imports down 10.1% and full exports down 2.8%. Domestic container volumes are down 0.4% year-to-date, with Alaska up 0.6% and Hawaii down 5.4%. Breakbulk remains a strong performer, with year-to-date October volumes of 345,075 metric tonnes, up 12.2% on robust industrial demand. Auto volumes of 224,416 units are down 2.2% year-to-date, with the tariff impact on the industry partly offset by a rise in vehicles diverted from Canada because of congestion. Washington United Terminals has been awarded a US$ 11.4 million Port Infrastructure Development Program grant, to be used for upgrading mooring bollards to suit larger container vessels and building concrete runways tailored to rubber-tired gantry cranes. Separately, HMM has announced a major investment at the terminal that will lift cargo-handling capacity from roughly 590,000 TEUs to 880,000 TEUs, including replacement of two ageing cranes and the addition of two rubber-tired gantry cranes, with equipment expected to be delivered and commissioned by 2028. Earlier in the year, US$ 2 million was announced for berth deepening at Washington United Terminals and Husky Terminal.

articles.summary: In order to enable the timely and efficient movement of export cargo, ocean common carriers transporting containerized cargo are required to file documented export policies as set forth in 46 CFR 542.1(j), issued as part of the Commission’s final rule…
articles.body: FMC Advisory — Documented Export Policies Must be Filed with the FMC by March 1 Each Year Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 Image courtesy FMC In order to enable the timely and efficient movement of export cargo, ocean common carriers transporting containerized cargo are required to file documented export policies as set forth in 46 CFR 542.1(j), issued as part of the Commission’s final rule, “Definition of Unreasonable Refusal to Deal or Negotiate with Respect to Vessel Space Accommodations Provided by an Ocean Common Carrier” issued in 2024. Common carriers must annually submit their documented export policy on or before March 1 each year. 90 FR 30 (Jan. 2, 2025); see also 46 CFR 542.1(j)(1). Failure to file as set forth below will constitute a violation of a federal regulation. Filing Instructions Unless superseded by subsequent Commission order or filing instructions issued by the Commission: 1. Ocean common carriers must file their documented export policy with the Commission on or before March 1 each calendar year. A documented export policy should cover the period until the next policy is due for submission. Common carriers may file updated versions more frequently as needed. 2. Documents must be submitted in English, and any monetary terms shall be expressed in terms of U.S. currency. 3. Documented export policies must be submitted via email to: [email protected] . 4. Each of the following items must be addressed in a documented export policy. The Commission provides the following guidance on how a carrier can best address each topic: “Pricing strategies” – The common carrier’s criteria for pricing export cargo space in service contracts, tariffs, and spot rates, detailing key cost drivers and their relative importance, including operational costs, vessel capacity utilization, equipment inventory levels, equipment repositioning and trade imbalance, as well as a discussion of how these factors are incorporated into pricing; whether customers are notified within a pre-determined timeframe, and details as to what that timeframe is, before any changes to freight rates, surcharges, or fees are implemented. “Markets served” and “Services offered” – (1) Each geographic/export market in which the common carrier offers service, in reasonable detail. (2) The export services the common carrier makes available within each market, including routes, sailing frequency, service alternatives/substitutes, and conditions for negotiating and accepting export bookings, especially to the extent such conditions differ from conditions applied to import bookings. “Strategies for equipment provision” – How the common carrier determines the availability, allocation, and positioning of equipment in support of exports, including empty containers; how equipment inventory is monitored and allocated across the market served, including how inventory distribution affects equipment availability; how equipment shortages or other disruptions may affect bookings and mitigation strategies in place to anticipate and address such issues; how the common carrier’s policies and practices for determining and maintaining an adequate supply of containers/equipment based on cargo volume, type, and transport costs in the markets served. “Blank sailings” – The common carrier’s definition of blank sailings, policy and practices for cancelling sailings, including the timing and all communication mechanisms for notifying shippers of such blankings, and mitigation strategies to assist with export cargo bookings affected by blankings; how the cascading effects across schedules and operations are addressed. “Sweeper vessels” – A detailed explanation of the common carrier’s rules, practices, policies and/or performance targets concerning the designation, and the use, of sweeper vessels. Under the regulation, a sweeper vessel “means a vessel exclusively designated to load and move empty containers from a U.S. port for the purpose of transporting them to another designated location.” “Alternative remedies or assistance” – A detailed explanation of the common carrier’s rules, practices, policies and/or performance targets for providing alternative vessel space accommodations to an export shipper denied space, including the circumstances under which each alternative is considered or offered. A detailed explanation of how affected export shippers can request assistance and where such resources are found on the carrier’s website. 5. If any topics listed under 541.2(j)(1)(i), 541.2(j)(1)(ii), and/or 541.2(j)(1)(iii) are not addressed in a documented export policy because they are not applicable, the documented export policy should attest to this inapplicability clearly and unambiguously and provide a detailed factual explanation for non-applicability. 6. Submissions must be signed by a duly authorized officer of the regulated party with a copy of evidence of the officer’s authority. Each documented export policy must clearly identify the common carrier’s: FMC organization number, legal name, and all associated trade name(s) if applicable. This ensures that documented export policies are properly accredited to the correct organization and that a common carrier is not deemed to be in violation of the regulation. A documented export policy of a parent company may cover subsidiary companies in addition to the parent company. However, the documented export policy must clearly identify for the parent company and each subsidiary covered: the FMC organization number, the legal name of the company, and all associated trade name(s), if applicable. Unless such information is clearly identified, the FMC will consider the submission as applicable only to the parent company. Documented export policies will not be circulated outside of the Federal Maritime Commission. These documents, and the information contained therein, are not publicly disclosable, in whole or in part, including in response to requests under the Freedom of Information Act. Failure to file a documented export policy by March 1 constitutes a violation of a federal regulation. A person that violates a regulation or order of the Commission is liable to the United States Government for a civil penalty. 46 U.S.C. 41107(a). “Each day of a continuing violation is a separate violation,” with a current maximum penalty of $14,988 per violation, or $74,943 where the violation was willful and knowing. Id.; 46 CFR 506.4(d). Additionally, submission of knowingly fraudulent statements or misrepresentation in response to this requirement, or any other regulation or agency order, can result in criminal prosecution under 18 U.S.C. 1001, which, upon conviction, carries criminal penalties of a fine, up to five years of imprisonment, or both.
takeaways: FMC Advisory — Documented Export Policies Must be Filed with the FMC by March 1 Each Year Maritime Activity Reports, Inc.
Common carriers must annually submit their documented export policy on or before March 1 each year.

articles.body: Euroseas reported net income attributable to controlling shareholders of US$25.6 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared with US$29.7 million during the same period last year. The containership owner generated net revenue of US$54.1 million, down 5% from US$56.9 million in the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA stood at US$38.3 million, slightly below the US$38.8 million recorded a year earlier. Adjusted net income attributable to controlling shareholders reached US$30.7 million. Basic and diluted adjusted earnings per share were US$4.39 and US$4.37, respectively. Euroseas operated an average of 21 vessels during the quarter, compared with 22 vessels a year earlier. Its average time charter equivalent rate increased by 1.4% to US$29,705 per vessel per day. Euroseas raises quarterly dividend The company declared a quarterly dividend of US$0.85 per share, representing an increase of US$0.05 per share. The dividend is expected to be paid on or around 16 December 2026 to shareholders of record as of 9 December. Euroseas has also repurchased 480,460 common shares since launching its share buyback programme in May 2022. The shares represent approximately 6.8% of the company’s outstanding stock and were acquired for a total of around US$11.36 million. “We are pleased to continue reporting solid results during the third quarter of 2026 despite one of our vessels having undergone drydocking in the process of being sold,” said Aristides Pittas, Chairman and CEO of Euroseas. Pittas said profitable charter contracts continued to support the company’s earnings. He added that feeder containership charter rates increased by between 5% and 10% from the beginning of the third quarter through mid-November. Euroseas has secured charter coverage of more than 90% for 2027 and almost 50% for 2028. Only two vessels are currently expected to require charter renewals around the middle of 2027. Nine-month adjusted EBITDA reaches US$119.3 million For the first nine months of 2026, Euroseas generated net revenue of US$166.4 million, compared with US$170.5 million in the corresponding period of 2025. Net income attributable to controlling shareholders reached US$91.4 million, while adjusted net income stood at US$96.5 million. Adjusted EBITDA increased to US$119.3 million from US$115.2 million a year earlier. The fleet achieved an average time charter equivalent rate of US$30,124 per day during the nine-month period, up from US$28,735 per day in the same period last year. Euroseas completed the sale of the 2,556 TEU EVRIDIKI G on 31 October for approximately US$26 million. The company expects to recognise a gain of around US$22.5 million from the transaction in its fourth-quarter results. Following the sale, Euroseas operates 20 containerships with a combined capacity of 58,588 TEU. Its fleet comprises 14 feeder vessels and six intermediate containerships. The company also has 12 newbuildings scheduled for delivery between the third quarter of 2027 and the first quarter of 2029. After their delivery, its fleet is expected to comprise 32 vessels with a combined capacity of 94,840 TEU.

articles.title: Floating Production Outlook: Pipeline Looks Huge, But Not All Projects Are Created Equal
articles.summary: Global floating hydrocarbons and electricity production and storage infrastructure (floating units) has a sizeable development pipeline through 2035, but the gap between identified projects and committed work is substantial. Intelatus Global Partners tracks 711 floating units worldwide…
articles.body: Floating Production Outlook: Pipeline Looks Huge, But Not All Projects Are Created Equal Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Alisa Reiner , Contributor Alisa Reiner is an independent contributor. Alisa brings experience in both... November 18, 2026 Figure 1. World map of selected installed and future pipeline floating units. Map note: The map covers 327 geographically assigned FPSO and FLNG units across all recorded years. Five Available units have no first-production year or geographic deployment and are excluded. Only countries with recorded FPSO/FLNG projects are shaded; darker red indicates larger regional totals. GOM = Gulf of Mexico, LATAM = Latin America, APAC = Asia-Pacific. Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Figure 2. Regional floating infrastructure composition by type, all recorded years. Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Figure 3. Floating units by region and status, all recorded years. Note: Five “Available” units have no geographic affiliation and are excluded from regional totals; Figures 1 and 2 therefore cover 706 units. Source: Floating Units Database, Intelatus Global Partners (October 2026); calculations by author. Figure 4. Planned and on-order floating units by expected first-production year, 2026–2035. Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Global floating hydrocarbons and electricity production and storage infrastructure (floating units) has a sizeable development pipeline through 2035, but the gap between identified projects and committed work is substantial. Intelatus Global Partners tracks 711 floating units worldwide, including 232 planned or on-order facilities with expected first-production dates in 2026–2035 . The commercial implications extend beyond floating unit construction. A deepwater FPSO in LATAM, a SEMI in the Gulf of Mexico, and an FSRU at a coastal terminal involve different mooring systems, installation sequences, and vessel requirements. For mooring suppliers and offshore support vessel owners, project maturity, water depth, and regional charter conditions will determine how much of the identified pipeline becomes executable work. A Large Fleet, but Not a Single Market Analysis covers 460 installed, 72 on order, 174 planned, and five available units. APAC leads the installed fleet with 137 units, followed by LATAM (93) and Africa (89). FPSOs account for 181 installed units, ahead of FSOs (74), FSRUs (48), and SEMIs (40) . APAC, LATAM, and Africa together account for 492 of the 711 recorded units, but their status mix distinguishes operating assets from prospective work (Figure 1). 174 planned units outnumber the 72 on order by more than two to one, and the main uncertainty is how much of that prospective work becomes contracted installations. Where the Units Are LATAM has 99 FPSOs among 145 units, whereas the Gulf of Mexico has 25 SEMIs and only ten FPSOs. The Mediterranean Sea is dominated by FSRUs (20 of 34 units), a different installation market from offshore production. \APAC has the largest regional fleet (217 units), spread across 74 FPSOs, 50 FSOs, 25 FSRUs, and other designs. Its 68 projects dated 2026–2035 span production, storage, and LNG import rather than one offshore installation profile. As for water depths, regional means are 1,564 m in LATAM, 1,402.3 m in the Gulf of Mexico, 889 m in Africa, 509 m in the Mediterranean Sea, 328 m in APAC, and 297 m in North Europe . However, APAC’s lower average masks considerable variation — Indonesia and India are emerging as markets for ultra-deepwater drilling. Yet a simple geographical unit count is an incomplete measure of supplier demand. Commercial interest is forward-looking. LATAM has 52 planned or on-order units dated 2026–2035, including 41 FPSOs; Brazil accounts for 30 projects and Guyana for 11. Its 21 units in 2031–2035 give it the largest regional pipeline for that later period. Africa has 41 planned or on-order units scheduled for 2026–2035, including 23 FPSOs and seven FLNG facilities. Nigeria accounts for 14 projects, while Namibia has six. All 13 African units dated 2031–2035 remain planned, so their conversion into installation work still depends on project sanction and procurement. The Gulf of Mexico features 21 planned or on-order units dated 2026–2035, including nine SEMIs, versus four FPSOs and four FLNG facilities. Its prospective installation mix therefore differs materially from FPSO-led LATAM. FPSOs Drive the Production Pipeline Of the 232 planned or on-order facilities dated 2026–2035, 108 are FPSOs (47%), compared with 30 FLNG units, 33 FSRUs, 15 SEMIs, and 17 FSOs (Table 1). The remaining 29 units are other floating infrastructure types. Unit type 2026–2030 2031–2035 Total FPSO 70 38 108 FLNG 16 14 30 SEMIs 8 7 15 FSRUs 29 4 33 FSOs 17 0 17 Other floating units 24 5 29 Total 164 68 232 Source: Intelatus Global Partners. Notably, interest in FLNG is broadening. Yinson Production , an established FPSO operator, is looking to extend its lease-and-operate model to FLNG, applying its experience in development, construction, and operations to offshore gas projects. In Brazil, Petrobras has sought market information on potential FLNG options for its offshore gas resources. Rystad Energy expects global FLNG capacity to rise from 14.1 Mtpa in 2024 to 42 Mtpa by 2030 and 55 Mtpa by 2035, supported by stronger operating performance and the economics of smaller or remote gas fields. The IEA projects more than 330 bcm/year of new LNG export capacity entering service over 2025–2030. This includes onshore plants as well as floating facilities, but the sheer scope is illustrative. T he Schedule Gets Less Certain After 2030 Expected first production peaks in 2028 at 52 units, evenly split between 26 on order and 26 planned (Figure 3). This is not the offshore installation peak: mooring pre-lay and floater hook-up normally occur before first production, and project delays could shift that workload across years. Project maturity is a greater uncertainty than the precise annual profile. Of the 164 units dated 2026–2030, 70 are on order and 94 are planned. In 2031–2035, just two are on order and 66 remain planned. Schedules can move, and some developments may never reach sanction. Conversely, newly added projects could increase demand after 2030. Importantly, the installed fleet is not a static base to which all pipeline projects can simply be added. Some units will retire; others will remain on their fields longer, be modified, or be redeployed. The database does not contain a complete schedule of retirements and redeployments, so the identified pipeline is not a forecast of net fleet growth. Similarly, redeployment does not necessarily require building a new hull, but it could involve repair, new moorings, underwater operations, and reinstatement. Mooring Design Determines Installation Scope Floater architecture and field conditions determine the mooring scope. A turret-moored FPSO, spread-moored SEMI, and tension-leg platform transmit station-keeping loads differently and require different installation sequences. Water depth, metocean loading, and seabed conditions affect mooring geometry, line length, strength, materials, and anchor choice, including whether drag-embedment, suction, or torpedo anchors are suitable. These choices set vessel and handling requirements. A typical deepwater chain–polyester–chain system can involve separate campaigns for anchor installation, line pre-lay, and floater hook-up. Installation loads and methods, rather than floater type alone, determine anchor handling tug supply (AHTS) vessels’ bollard pull, winch and deck capacity, and the number of loadouts required. A single development can therefore generate work across floating facilities, moorings, and subsea systems. For suppliers, this makes a combined assessment of floater type and regional conditions essential — it is their interaction that determines the technical specifications of mooring systems, installation requirements, and ultimately the type and capacity of offshore support vessels (OSV) needed. Charter Markets Shape OSV Availability Market factors also matter. Charter terms can restrict the pool of suitable vessels for other projects. For instance, in Brazil, DOF secured four-year awards for four AHTS vessels, including one with more than 350 tons of bollard pull and three configured for deepwater remotely operated vehicle (ROV) vessel work. Such long-term commitments secure utilization for owners while limiting high-specification vessel availability elsewhere. North Sea vessel tightness in 2025-2026 has been partly linked to longer Brazilian commitments. Conversely, West Africa is more short-term campaign-driven: vessels often get mobilized there from the North Sea, moving south during the northern hemisphere winter. Summer returns are possible, not automatic; mobilization costs, contract terms, local requirements, and weather windows govern the economics. The Commercial Outlook The key message is that the floating market should be read as a portfolio of very different offshore campaigns rather than a single global trend. LATAM remains the deepest pool of FPSO demand, but it is also one of the markets where large, long-duration projects can tie up high-specification tonnage and absorb substantial mooring scope. APAC is broader and less uniform: it combines production, storage, and gas infrastructure, while parts of the region are now moving further into deepwater. Africa offers both established FPSO work and a growing gas-related story, but much of the later pipeline still has to convert from planning into funded execution. For suppliers, that means market entry should be based on technical fit and regional positioning, not just on the headline number of units. The more forward-looking point is that project quality now matters more than project count. The 2026–2030 pipeline contains the bulk of identified near-term work, but after 2030 the market becomes more gas-heavy and much less certain, with most units still only planned. That creates a premium for companies that can screen pipelines early, follow the shift from concept to commitment, and match vessels, moorings, and installation methods to the projects most likely to move. In practice, the winners are likely to be those positioned where three conditions overlap: a credible project backlog, technical complexity that limits competition, and local market access. That is where floating-unit activity turns into real commercial demand. articles.summary: Israeli containership operator ZIM Integrated Shipping Services reported a sharp increase in third-quarter 2026 earnings, driven by stronger freight rates, higher cargo volumes and improved operating margins, prompting the company to raise its…
articles.body: ZIM Q3 Profit Surges to $830M as Freight Rates Rise 55% Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 Image Credit Wellington Luck Chen Lichtenstein, CEO, ZIM. Photo Credit Shlomo Shoham Israeli containership operator ZIM Integrated Shipping Services reported a sharp increase in third-quarter 2026 earnings, driven by stronger freight rates, higher cargo volumes and improved operating margins, prompting the company to raise its full-year financial guidance. ZIM reported third-quarter revenue of $2.71 billion, up 53% from $1.78 billion a year earlier. Net income surged to $830 million from $123 million, while adjusted EBITDA more than doubled to $1.33 billion. The company carried 962,000 TEUs during the quarter, a 4% year-over-year increase, while average freight rates climbed 55% to $2,480 per TEU from $1,602. Adjusted EBIT reached $993 million, representing a 37% margin, compared with 15% in the corresponding 2025 period. “By keeping our network agile and focusing on premium, profitable trades, we are supporting our customers and positioning ZIM for further growth,” said Chen Lichtenstein, ZIM President and CEO. ZIM also generated $1.22 billion in quarterly free cash flow, strengthening its balance sheet and reducing net debt to $1.86 billion. Fleet Development and Orderbook ZIM currently operates 112 containerships with aggregate capacity of approximately 703,000 TEUs, alongside 13 car carriers. During the second half of 2026, the company took delivery of two newly built 8,000-TEU containerships under five-to-seven-year charters. Its charter orderbook includes 56 vessels, comprising 52 containerships totaling approximately 418,000 TEUs and four car carriers. The newbuilding program includes 18 LNG dual-fuel containerships of 11,500 TEUs each. ZIM also expanded its service network, launching the ZX3 expedited Asia–U.S. West Coast service and Falcon service connecting China with Argentina and southern Brazil. Reflecting stronger market conditions, ZIM raised its 2026 adjusted EBITDA forecast to $3.3 billion–$3.5 billion, from $2.7 billion–$3 billion previously. Meanwhile, Hapag-Lloyd's proposed $35-per-share acquisition of ZIM remains subject to regulatory approvals, including Israeli government consent. The transaction is targeted for completion in the first quarter of 2027. ZIM declared a dividend of $2.01 per share, totaling approximately $243 million.

articles.title: NYK Names Gas Carrier with Ammonia-Fueled Engines Izanami
articles.summary: Japan's NYK has named Izanami, a newly built 40,000-cu.m. medium gas carrier equipped with ammonia-fueled main and auxiliary engines, marking a milestone in the development of ammonia propulsion for commercial shipping.Built at Japan Marine…
articles.body: NYK Names Gas Carrier with Ammonia-Fueled Engines Izanami Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 18, 2026 Image courtesy NYK Japan's NYK has named Izanami, a newly built 40,000-cu.m. medium gas carrier equipped with ammonia-fueled main and auxiliary engines, marking a milestone in the development of ammonia propulsion for commercial shipping. Built at Japan Marine United Corporation's Ariake Shipyard in Kumamoto Prefecture, the vessel was named November 6 by NYK President Takaya Soga , followed by an unveiling ceremony November 17. According to NYK, Izanami is the world's first vessel equipped with ammonia-fueled engines for both propulsion and onboard power generation. The ship features a dual-fuel, two-stroke main engine manufactured by Japan Engine Corporation and dual-fuel, four-stroke auxiliary engines supplied by IHI Power Systems. The 180-meter vessel has a breadth of 32 meters and molded depth of 18.45 meters and will operate under the Japanese flag. The project is part of Japan's New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) Green Innovation Fund , established to accelerate the development and commercialization of technologies supporting carbon neutrality by 2050. NYK, Japan Engine Corporation, IHI Power Systems and Nihon Shipyard were selected for the program in October 2021. Working with classification society ClassNK , the partners have developed domestically produced ammonia propulsion technology for commercial vessels. Following delivery, Izanami will be time-chartered to Yara Clean Ammonia Switzerland SA , part of Norway's Yara International . The charter will include demonstration voyages to evaluate engine performance, operational safety and greenhouse gas reductions under actual operating conditions. Although ammonia combustion produces no carbon dioxide, its use as marine fuel presents technical challenges involving toxicity, fuel handling and emissions management. The operational trials will provide data to support future ammonia-fueled vessel development. The project builds on NYK's experience with Sakigake, an ammonia-fueled tugboat that entered commercial service in August 2024, also developed under the NEDO program. With Izanami moving into operation, NYK and its partners will transition from engine and vessel development to collecting performance data from commercial voyages, supporting efforts to establish ammonia as a viable alternative marine fuel for deep-sea shipping.

articles.title: Orlen spreads its wings across Central and Eastern Europe with new gas pacts
articles.summary: U.S. LNG is expected to reach more European energy markets as Orlen’s new partnerships strengthen regional cooperation.
articles.body: Collaboration November 18, 2026 · 4 minutes ago Orlen spreads its wings across Central and Eastern Europe with new gas pacts U.S. LNG is expected to reach more European energy markets as Orlen’s new partnerships strengthen regional cooperation. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email LNG carrier Source: Orlen Orlen, a Polish multi-sector company, is expanding its gas business across Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs) through new agreements and partnerships with energy companies in Ukraine, Slovakia and Hungary, highlighting Poland’s growing role as a regional gateway for global gas supplies and the firm’s ambitions to strengthen energy security while expanding its commercial footprint across the region. Orlen has revealed that it will supply Ukraine with natural gas from three LNG cargoes under a new contract with Naftogaz. This gas will originate from the United States and, following regasification at the LNG terminal in Świnoujście, will be transported via gas pipelines to Ukraine. The agreement, which will ensure the continuity of gas supplies to the Ukrainian market in the first quarter of 2027, is of significant importance in strengthening the energy security of the region, according to the Polish player. " Thanks to our continuously developing commercial expertise, our own LNG transport vessels and access to regasification capacity, we can effectively support Ukraine in diversifying its sources and routes of natural gas supply. This is particularly important in the face of growing threats to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Our activities strengthen the region’s energy security whilst delivering tangible business benefits. " — Robert Soszyński Vice President of the Orlen Management Board for Operations Orlen has been developing its commercial partnership with Naftogaz since 2025. During this time, the companies have concluded five contracts for the supply of over 600 million cubic meters of gas derived from the regasification of U.S. LNG imported to the terminals in Świnoujście and Klaipėda. " Our strategic partnership with Orlen allows us to secure US LNG supplies in the first quarter of 2027 and provide additional resilience during peak periods of winter gas demand. Amid ongoing Russian attacks, alongside our efforts to protect and restore our facilities, we are working to secure reliable sources and routes of gas supply. " — Sergii Fedorenko Acting Chief Executive Officer of Naftogaz Related Articles Clean Fuel Orlen and Naftogaz deepen energy ties with two MoUs 2 min read Orlen and Slovakia’s Slovenský plynárenský priemysel (SPP) have also signed an agreement revolving around a wider choice of gas sources for Slovakia and new sales opportunities for the Polish player, opening a new phase of talks on gas supplies using LNG imported into Poland. " We want to turn our experience in LNG sourcing and gas trading into new sales opportunities in Central and Eastern Europe. The agreement with SPP, Slovakia’s largest energy supplier, opens up the prospect of working with a partner of key importance to this market. Our goal is clear: to grow Orlen’s business and develop a competitive offering that gives our partners greater flexibility in purchasing gas. In this way, we combine our commercial ambitions with the region’s energy security. " — Ireneusz Fąfara President of the Management Board of Orlen The cooperation is based on LNG, which, once delivered to a terminal in Poland and regasified, could reach SPP through European gas networks. The talks will cover gas sources, commercial terms, and delivery arrangements. The partnership gives the duo flexibility to tailor their offering to market needs. The agreement also aligns with the objectives of REPowerEU, representing the EU’s plan to end dependence on Russian fossil fuels through energy savings, the development of renewable energy sources, and supply diversification, requiring a need to build commercial relationships with alternative suppliers and expand access to gas from a variety of sources. " SPP is intensively preparing for the period beyond 2027, when imports of Russian natural gas into the European Union will be phased out in accordance with REPowerEU legislation. Our priority is to ensure reliable and competitively priced natural gas supplies for our customers under these new conditions. Poland and Orlen represent a promising opportunity to further diversify our supply portfolio. The use of LNG terminals in Poland could provide Slovakia with access to additional natural gas sources on the global market while expanding the options for transporting gas to our country. " — Martin Húska Chief Executive Officer and Member of the Board of Directors of SPP Related Articles Clean Fuel EU endorses ban on Russian pipeline gas and LNG imports 3 min read Meanwhile, Orlen and Hungary’s MVM ONEnergy have signed a memorandum on potential cooperation in LNG deliveries to Polish terminals, regasification, and the transportation of natural gas to Hungary to assess solutions that support the security and diversification of gas supplies. Advertisement " Energy security in Central and Eastern Europe requires diverse gas supply sources and transportation routes, as well as cooperation between partners across the region. In our discussions with MVM ONEnergy, we want to draw on Orlen’s experience in LNG sourcing and organizing gas deliveries to European markets. The memorandum with MVM ONEnergy brings together two important objectives for us: strengthening the region’s energy security and expanding Orlen’s presence in the Hungarian market. " — Fąfara underlined. articles.title: Port of Savannah container volumes surge 25% in October
articles.summary: The Port of Savannah handled 565,366 TEUs in October 2026, an increase of 25% compared with the same month last year, according to the Georgia Ports Authority (GPA). The result marked the second-highest monthly container volume in the port’s history, supported by strong consumer demand and an extended peak shipping...
articles.body: The Port of Savannah handled 565,366 TEUs in October 2026, an increase of 25% compared with the same month last year, according to the Georgia Ports Authority (GPA). The result marked the second-highest monthly container volume in the port’s history, supported by strong consumer demand and an extended peak shipping season. Container throughput for fiscal year 2027 to date increased by 7.8%, representing an additional 152,991 TEUs compared with the corresponding period a year earlier. Vessel traffic also increased, with Savannah handling 160 ships during October, up 5% year-on-year. “Our container volumes are driven by strong consumer spending, an extended peak shipping season and our port and inland infrastructure ease of use,” said Griff Lynch, CEO, Georgia Ports Authority. Suez Canal routings support transit-time improvements Georgia Ports also highlighted changes in ocean carrier routings as a factor influencing supply chain performance. According to Kevin Price, President of Georgia Ports Authority, some shipping lines are returning to routes through the Suez Canal, potentially shortening transit times to Savannah. “We’re seeing ocean carriers return to Suez Canal routings which translate to 10-12 day transit improvements to Savannah supply chain inventory and fulfillment speeds, which is always welcome at this time of year with holiday sales and ecommerce ordering,” said Price. The authority expects container demand to remain strong through the end of the year, supported by holiday-related imports and e-commerce activity. Terminal investments support future capacity Alongside the increase in container volumes, Georgia Ports continues to develop infrastructure to accommodate future growth. The authority recently secured a permit from the US Army Corps of Engineers for the planned US$2.3 billion Savannah Container Terminal. The proposed facility will cover approximately 350 acres and provide an additional 3.5 million TEUs of annual capacity. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2028. Once completed, the development is expected to increase Savannah’s total container handling capacity to 12 million TEUs annually. Meanwhile, the US$1.6 billion renovation of Ocean Terminal is more than 60% complete. The project will increase the terminal’s annual capacity from 200,000 TEUs to 1.75 million TEUs. According to GPA, truck gate construction and associated support services are 99% complete. The authority is also working with the US Army Corps of Engineers on a study examining possible channel deepening and additional passing areas for two-way vessel traffic. Inland connectivity remains another focus. The Gainesville Inland Port held its official opening ceremony on 10 November, strengthening rail-linked logistics infrastructure serving Georgia’s manufacturing and distribution markets. The latest October figures underline Savannah’s growing role in US East Coast container trade as the port prepares for additional cargo-handling capacity.

articles.body: Europe Offshore Neo Next+ snaps up EnQuest’s North Sea business in $960m deal Bojan Lepic November 18, 2026 0 345 1 minute read EnQuest EnQuest UK offshore producer Neo Next+ Energy has agreed to acquire EnQuest’s entire UK upstream oil and gas business in a deal worth up to $960m, further consolidating its position as the largest producer on the UK Continental Shelf. The transaction involves acquiring EnQuest Britain Limited for $840m in upfront cash, with a further $120m potentially payable depending on oil prices and changes to the UK’s Energy Profits Levy. The portfolio includes producing interests in the operated Kraken, Magnus, and Greater Kittiwake Area fields, alongside a non-operated stake in Golden Eagle. The deal also covers the undeveloped Bressay and Bentley discoveries and infrastructure including the Sullom Voe Terminal, Northern Leg Gas Pipeline, and Ninian Pipeline system. The assets produced approximately 31,100 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2025, with 92% coming from liquids. At the end of last year, the portfolio held 122m barrels of oil equivalent in proven and probable reserves and 308m barrels in contingent resources. Neo Next+ executive chair John Knight said the acquisition would strengthen the company’s scale, production base and cash flow while supporting further consolidation of the UK offshore industry. The deal follows a series of major transactions by the company, which completed its merger with Repsol’s UK upstream business in July 2025 before combining with TotalEnergies’ British offshore operations in March 2026. Meanwhile, the disposal marks a major strategic shift for EnQuest, which is increasingly concentrating on Southeast Asia. In June, the company announced acquisitions worth up to $833m covering interests in four production sharing contracts offshore Malaysia. After completing those transactions and the UK disposal, EnQuest expects its Southeast Asian operations to produce around 70,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, based on 2025 figures. EnQuest will retain its Veri Energy business and associated carbon capture interests. The North Sea transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and completion of EnQuest’s Malaysian acquisitions. articles.body: Containers Europe Offen firms up four-ship boxship comeback in China Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 860 1 minute read GSI GSI German tonnage provider Claus-Peter Offen has reportedly firmed up all four of its planned 7,000 teu containership newbuildings, ending a nearly two-decade absence from the ordering market. Shipbuilding sources say the Hamburg-based owner has committed to the full quartet after initially signing a letter of intent in September for two firm vessels and two options. China’s Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI), part of state-owned CSSC, remains linked to the deal, although the builder has yet to be formally confirmed. No contract price or firm delivery dates have emerged, with earlier market reports pointing to slots around 2030. The conventionally powered ships would add around 28,000 teu to Offen’s fleet and mark its first containership orders since 2007. Market sources have also suggested that the four vessels have secured charter backing from one of the world’s ten largest liner operators. The charterer’s identity and employment terms have not been disclosed. The newbuildings fall into a segment where Chinese yards have attracted growing interest from both liner operators and tonnage providers. One of the designs gaining traction is SDARI’s compact Sealion 7100, which measures 255 m in length and 42.8 m in breadth, with capacity for up to 1,143 reefer containers. The final specification of Offen’s ships has not been confirmed. For comparison, South Korea’s Namsung Shipping has recently been linked to two firm 7,100 teu ships plus two options at China’s Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Corporation, with brokers putting the price at around $89m per vessel. Offen’s return to ordering follows years of relying on older tonnage, much of it employed by major liners including MSC and Ocean Network Express. Its last containership newbuilding programme dates back to before the 2008 financial crisis, with the final vessels arriving several years later after construction delays. Among the youngest ships stemming from that earlier investment are the 2012-built, 5,574 teu MSC Coruna and MSC Vigo, both still listed in the company’s fleet under MSC employment. Founded in 1971, Offen remains one of Germany’s largest non-operating containership owners, with its website listing more than 40 vessels under management. articles.body: Interconnectors November 18, 2026 · 1 minute ago Greece: Dodecanese islands' link to mainland awarded €228.9 million EU grant NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Source: CINEA An interconnector that will link Greece's Dodecanese islands to the mainland electricity grid has secured the largest grant ever awarded under the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency's (CINEA) European Public Sector Loan Facility program, amounting to €228.9 million. The interconnection will be delivered in two phases, with the first to include a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) submarine link between the mainland point in Corinth and the island of Kos, together with two AC/DC converter stations and the associated transmission infrastructure. With an estimated budget of €2.54 billion, phase 1 is supported under the Public Sector Loan Facility (PSLF) through a €228.9 million EU grant combined with a €1.53 billion loan from the European Investment Bank (EIB), representing the largest contribution to a single project under the PSLF to date. The first project phase also benefits from a €534 million grant from the Greek Decarbonisation Fund. “The Dodecanese interconnection project is an excellent example of how Greece, the European Commission and the European Investment Bank can work together to turn clean energy ambitions into reality,” said European Commission Directorate-General for Regional and Urban Policy Director Emma Toledano . “It will make a real difference to island communities, bringing them a cheaper and more reliable electricity supply while making it easier to use more renewable energy from a larger and more flexible grid. In doing so, the project shows what a socially just energy transition can look like in practice.” Related Articles Interconnectors Nexans to deliver 420 kilometers of cable for Greek interconnection 1 min read According to CINEA, Phase 1 alone is expected to cut CO2 emissions by around 7.7 million tons over 25 years, roughly 309,000 tons per year. By connecting the islands to the mainland grid, the project will also open the way for more renewable energy in the region, contributing directly to the energy and climate objectives of both the EU and Greece. The project's second phase, which is not part of the EU-supported project, will add AC interconnections to bring Rhodes and Karpathos into the system. Once completed, the two phases will end the Dodecanese islands’ electrical isolation, relieve grid saturation and allow polluting oil-fired power plants to be decommissioned. “The Dodecanese electricity interconnection project, currently being implemented by IPTO, will permanently end the region’s energy isolation, accelerate the phase-out of polluting oil-fired power plants, and unlock the renewable energy potential of the Aegean Sea," said Manos Manousakis , Chairman and CEO of the Greek transmission system operator (TSO), Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO). "The investment not only strengthens security of supply, but also lowers consumer costs, drives sustainable economic growth, and ensures a more resilient, interconnected grid across every corner of Greece. Securing the largest grant awarded to date under this EU funding program – alongside crucial backing from EIB and the Greek Decarbonisation Fund - marks a major milestone in our country’s energy transition." articles.title: Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges
articles.summary: Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions. The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the...
articles.body: Environment Operations Regulatory Shipping heavyweights warn against double carbon charges Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 461 2 minutes read IMO IMO Nine of the world’s leading shipping associations have joined forces to push governments towards a global emissions deal, warning that a patchwork of regional regulations risks leaving shipowners paying multiple times for the same carbon emissions. The joint intervention comes ahead of a crucial round of talks at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) later this month, with governments still divided over how to regulate and price shipping’s greenhouse gas emissions. BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), Intercargo, Intertanko, the World Shipping Council, Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), Interferry, the International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA) and the International Parcel Tankers Association (IPTA) have called for a single global framework that applies equally to vessels regardless of flag, ownership or trade. “Shipping is a global industry requiring global rules applied equally to all ships,” the organisations said. The groups warned that national and regional schemes could result in duplicated compliance requirements and multiple charges for the same emissions, undermining efforts to establish a level playing field. They want an IMO agreement that rewards verifiable emissions reductions while giving shipowners sufficient flexibility to manage the transition to cleaner fuels, many of which remain commercially unavailable for much of the existing fleet. The joint statement also calls for regulations that are fuel- and technology-neutral, enforceable and backed by clear incentives for investment in alternative fuels and energy-saving technologies. The intervention comes after the IMO failed to secure agreement on its proposed Net-Zero Framework in October 2025, forcing governments to postpone adoption for a year. The framework, which combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism, remains the subject of negotiations over its cost, design and implementation. The industry’s latest appeal follows growing concern over the spread of regional carbon schemes. Several African governments are moving towards their own shipping emissions charges, while European operators already face the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations. The nine associations warned that the lack of regulatory certainty is complicating investment decisions for shipowners, ports, fuel producers and financiers, particularly given the limited availability and high cost of lower-emissions fuels. Governments will resume negotiations at the IMO’s greenhouse gas working group from November 23 to 27, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session from November 30 to December 3. A further extraordinary session to consider adoption of the emissions framework could take place on December 4, subject to confirmation during MEPC 85. articles.body: Europe Offshore Renewables DEME orders pair of autonomous offshore survey vessels Bojan Lepic November 18, 2026 0 530 1 minute read DEMCON DEMCON Belgian marine contractor DEME has ordered two uncrewed offshore survey vessels from Dutch technology specialist DEMCON Unmanned Systems, expanding its capabilities in remote and autonomous offshore operations. The vessels will be based on DEMCON’s DUS OV platform, which incorporates a DNV type-approved design and technology intended to support certification for autonomous operations. The two units are already under construction, with delivery scheduled for 2027. Designed for multi-day offshore deployment, the vessels can operate directly from ports or be launched from larger offshore construction vessels. Their modular construction allows them to be transported internationally in standard shipping containers, providing flexibility when mobilising for survey campaigns. The contract also includes launch-and-recovery equipment, vessel-handling systems, and the integration of DEME’s survey instruments and communications technology. The new vessels will be equipped with DEMCON’s autonomous navigation and mission management software, supporting survey-route following, collision avoidance, dynamic positioning and remote intervention. A dedicated remote operations centre will allow personnel to monitor vessel systems, navigation, survey equipment, and operational performance. The design incorporates redundant propulsion, power, navigation and communication systems to maintain control in the event of individual equipment failures. DEMCON said the vessels were being developed in response to increasing demand for remote survey operations across offshore wind and marine infrastructure projects. The two companies are currently undertaking detailed engineering and systems integration work ahead of testing and delivery next year. articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Greater China CSSC Shipping adds two bulkers and takes over ASL boxship pair Adis Ajdin November 18, 2026 0 808 1 minute read Hong Kong-listed CSSC Shipping has signed up for another two 80,000 dwt grain carriers in China while moving to take over a pair of containership newbuildings from ASL Shipping in a combined HK$1.73bn ($221m) transaction. The ship leasing arm of state-owned China Shipbuilding Group has entered into two new contracts with Chengxi Shipyard and China Shipbuilding Trading, with Chengxi and CSSC Guangxi jointly responsible for building the vessels. Each bulker is priced at CNH326m ($49.3m), putting the latest two-ship commitment at CNH652m ($98.6m). The vessels are scheduled for completion by the end of 2029 and 2030, respectively. The fresh orders come just over two months after CSSC Shipping signed for ten 80,000 dwt bulkers at the same shipbuilding group in a CNH3.235bn ($481m) deal. The additional pair takes the company’s grain carrier programme to 12 vessels, subject to the necessary approvals. Alongside the bulker contracts, CSSC Shipping has agreed to shift two existing 5,300 teu containership orders at Guangzhou Wenchong into CA Shipping, its joint venture with ASL Navigation. The vessels were originally contracted by ASL Shipping . Under novation agreements, CA Shipping will assume the original buyer’s rights and obligations. The contracts are worth $61.4m per ship, or $122.8m combined, with construction scheduled for completion in September and November 2028. CA Shipping is 60% owned by CSSC Shipping subsidiary Fortune Vcontainer Carriers, with the remaining 40% held by ASL Navigation, a subsidiary of ASL Shipping. Both transactions remain subject to independent shareholder approval and the effectiveness of the associated bareboat charter agreements. If the containership novations fail to take effect by January 31, 2027, the original contracts will remain with ASL Shipping. CSSC Shipping said it plans to finance the package through internal resources and bank borrowings, with the vessels intended to generate leasing income.
